activity: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
knowledge_domain: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
fact: The USDA calls 4 to 60 degrees Celsius (40 to 140 degrees Fahrenheit) the danger zone, the range where bacteria in food multiply rapidly.
story:
The walk-in door of Ms. Ito's restaurant stuck unless you lifted it and pushed at the same time, and Aidan had learned this on his first Sunday, when he stood in the alley with a grocery bag sweating through his T-shirt and felt like an impostor. By the fourth Sunday he did it without thinking. Inside, the kitchen was spartan and immaculate, steel counters wiped down, knives racked by size, the walk-in humming its one low note, and Ms. Ito would look up from whatever she was portioning and nod at the empty station by the ovens, which was her way of saying it was his.

He had asked her for the space because his mother had started working the late shift, and their dinners had become a rotation of frozen things reheated at odd hours, the two of them crossing in the kitchen at ten p.m. like strangers sharing a hostel. He wanted to learn to cook a whole week at once, five dinners made on Sunday and parceled into containers, so that when his mother came home there would be something waiting that did not come from a box with an illustration on it. Ms. Ito had listened to all of this while boning a chicken, and when he finished she had said only, "Then make a list, and buy only what is on it." He had taken this as scripture, or nearly. He let himself deviate once, for a jar of pickled jalapeños that spoke to him from the shelf.

The planning was the part nobody warned him about. At home, at his desk, with a legal pad and his phone's calculator open, he tried to convert seven days into arithmetic: if the chicken thighs were on sale in family packs, and the beans came dry by the pound, then Sunday's two hours of cooking could buy Thursday's twenty free minutes. It felt like a kind of affidavit, this list, a signed promise between his intentions and his money. He had forty-two dollars. Anything not on the list was perjury.

On the fourth Sunday, Tyra came with him. She had a shift bussing tables at the restaurant and had started lingering afterward, ostensibly to steal leftovers, actually, Aidan suspected, because the kitchen was warm and lit and her own house was neither. She sat on an upturned milk crate while he browned ground turkey and onions in the wide pan, and she read his list aloud in the voice of a customs officer. "'Two cans crushed tomatoes, item eight, subtotal thirty-one ten.' Very menacing." She peeled an orange she had not paid for. "You're doing a whole week in one pot? That's either genius or a hostage situation."

He explained the logic as he stirred: cook in batches, cool them, refrigerate them, reheat them one night at a time, and the week assembled itself in advance instead of collapsing nightly into cereal. It was, he was realizing, a way of moving effort to a day when he had effort to spare. Tyra said it sounded like the opposite of how she did anything, which he suspected was a compliment.

The chili was the centerpiece, the biggest batch, the thing he was proudest of, so of course it was the thing that betrayed him. He got the containers washed and the turkey divided and the rice portioned, and then Ms. Ito called him to help carry a delivery, and then Tyra showed him a video on her phone that was somehow eleven minutes long, and somewhere in the middle of all that the enormous pot of chili came off the heat and sat. He did not think about it. He boxed the smaller things, thanked Ms. Ito, and went home with everything packed in his mother's cooler bags, the big pot riding in the back because it would not fit in containers until he bought more. He left it, lidded, on the kitchen table, and went to bed pleased with himself.

At two in the morning his mother came home, and in the morning the pot was still there, and Tyra, who had arrived early to help label containers before his shift, stood over it with her arms crossed like a health inspector who had seen things. "How long was this out?"

"Since like eight. Nine, maybe."

"Nine at night to now is, what, fourteen hours." She lifted the lid and peered in, and the chili looked fine, honestly, looked rich and red and better than anything he had ever made. That was the sinister part. She ruminated a moment, tapping the spoon against the pot's rim. "I actually know this. Foods class, sophomore year. The USDA calls 4 to 60 degrees Celsius the danger zone, 40 to 140 Fahrenheit. That's the range where bacteria in food multiply rapidly. Room temperature is right in the middle of it."

He wanted to argue that the lid was on, that it smelled fine, that people left soup out all the time, that his grandmother had left a pot of stew on the back of the stove for what appeared to be entire presidencies. But he could hear the words arranging themselves against him: fourteen hours, danger zone, multiply rapidly. He had made a list with the care of a lawyer and then left the main exhibit sitting out like a fool. "The whole week's worth," he said. "That's five dinners."

"That's five dinners," Tyra agreed, with the gentleness of someone confirming a diagnosis. She was already taking the pot toward the sink, and he watched the chili go, all that arithmetic, that Sunday, those forty-two dollars, sliding toward the drain. He had one container of turkey and rice that had made it into the fridge, and a plan for Thursday that now involved toast.

His mother, informed by text, replied with a single laughing-crying emoji and the message "proud of you anyway, weirdo," which he read four times. That evening he was back in Ms. Ito's kitchen, before his shift, writing a new list at the steel counter while she portioned fish and pretended not to notice that the pot he was returning was empty and freshly washed. At the top of the list he wrote, in capital letters, COOL IT FAST, FRIDGE BY NINE, and underlined it twice. Tyra leaned over his shoulder.

"Adding pickled jalapeños this time?"

activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
knowledge_domain: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
fact: One month of free rent on a twelve-month lease at 1,200 dollars a month lowers the effective monthly rent to 1,100 dollars.
story:
Joseph had told everyone, twice, that he understood leases completely, and by the second telling he almost believed it himself. He sat on the folding table at the Spin Cycle Laundromat with two printouts in front of him and a pencil that kept rolling toward the edge whenever the dryer below him shuddered into its spin cycle. His mother's sheets were in that dryer. She was working the late shift, and she had left him the papers and a question she hadn't asked out loud, which was whether he could be trusted with it.

The first lease was for the Marlowe, a building he had toured once and liked more than he wanted to admit, all new carpet and a lobby that smelled faintly of lemon. The second was for a smaller place on Delancey Street, cheaper by the month, and his mother had circled that number twice. Then the Marlowe's agent had sent a follow-up email with a line about a move-in special, one month free, and Joseph had circled nothing because he didn't yet know what he was looking at.

"You're doing homework at a laundromat," said Jeremy, who came through the door with a duffel bag and the weary posture of someone whose washing machine had died on Sunday. "That's the saddest thing I've seen all week, and I watched our team lose by thirty."

"It's not homework." Joseph slid one page across the table. "It's real. Look at this and tell me which apartment is cheaper."

Jeremy dropped his duffel, looked at the papers with the expression of a stoic facing a long afternoon, and said, "The Delancey one. It says right there. Lower number, cheaper apartment. That's how numbers work."

Joseph had been certain of the same thing an hour ago. That was the trouble, or part of it. He liked being certain, and he had discovered this summer that being certain and being right were not always the same animal, though they could look alike from a distance. The move-in special captivated him precisely because it didn't announce itself. It sat in one line of an email, quiet, the way a canny poker player sits on a good hand.

He wrote on the back of the Marlowe flyer. Eleven payments, he thought, because one month of the twelve didn't cost anything, and then he divided by all twelve anyway. The pencil hovered. He did it twice because the first time felt like it had to be wrong, like he'd smuggled a number in that didn't belong.

"Wait," he said. "The Marlowe. One month of free rent on a twelve-month lease at twelve hundred a month, and it comes out to eleven hundred a month. The real rent. The whole rent, spread out."

"So it's still more than Delancey," Jeremy said, loading a machine.

"That's what I can't tell." Joseph pulled out his phone and found the Delancey listing again. It said nothing about heat. It said nothing about water. The Marlowe email mentioned an allowance for electricity, which sounded generous until he noticed it was an allowance, a ceiling, a thing you could go over. He thought about calling each office and asking what utilities cost, and then he thought about how the person answering the phone at a leasing office might have reasons to round in a flattering direction.

Allie arrived for her mother's comforters ten minutes later, took one look at his papers, and asked the question he'd been avoiding. "Have you actually called anyone, or are you just reading?"

"Reading is research," Joseph said.

"Reading is hiding." She sat down across from him. "Call about the utilities. Otherwise you're comparing one real number and one imaginary number, and you're going to pick the imaginary one because it's nicer."

Ms. Wu, who ran the change machine and had watched Joseph fold laundry there since he was eleven, drifted over with a clipboard and said nothing, which from her was a form of attention. The dryers roared. Joseph dialed the Marlowe, and a woman told him the allowance covered electricity but not the overage from running the air conditioner all summer, and then he dialed Delancey, where a man said heat was included but the hot water heater was " temperamental," which Joseph understood to mean not included in the way that mattered.

He wrote the numbers in the margin of the flyer, though not all of them were numbers. Some were just words with costs hiding inside them, like "temperamental" and "overage." He found that he liked this, the slow taking apart, and he also found it slightly frightening, because the two buildings wouldn't line up into a single clean answer the way problems at school did. At school the answer was either right or wrong and then you went home. Here, the Delancey was cheaper if the winter was mild, and the Marlowe was cheaper if it wasn't, and no one would tell him in advance what kind of winter it would be.

"So which one?" Jeremy asked, back from the machines with a slushie he'd bought from the vending machine against all reason.

"I don't know yet," Joseph said, and was surprised by how little it hurt to say it. "The free month makes the Marlowe eleven hundred a month instead of twelve hundred. That part I'm sure of. Everything after that is a guess about weather."

"That's a boring answer," said Jeremy.

"It's the true one." He straightened the papers, squared their edges against the table, and slid them into the folder his mother had left him. The dryer buzzed behind him, and Ms. Wu marked something on her clipboard, and Joseph went to pull out his mother's sheets, which had come out warm and would need folding while he still had the table, which was the one thing in the whole evening he knew how to do.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: The 26th Amendment, which set the US voting age at 18, was ratified in 1971 in about three months, faster than any other amendment.
story:
The line at the community hall moved faster than Logan expected, which somehow disappointed him. He had wanted the wait, the small civic delay, a chance to feel the weight of the thing arriving. Instead a volunteer with a clipboard found his name in under a minute and pointed him toward a folding table where a woman handed him a ballot without looking up. He was eighteen years and twenty-six days old, and this was his first election.

He had almost not come. Two nights ago, at his grandmother's table, the argument had started over meatloaf, his uncle saying voting was pointless in their district, the outcome already decided, and Logan had said, maybe to provoke, that if it was so pointless why did people fight about it. His grandmother set down her fork. When she was eighteen, she said, she couldn't have voted at all. Logan had stared at her. She was born in 1952, which he did in his head, which made her eighteen in 1970, which meant... what? He had always assumed eighteen was just how it worked, like the age for everything.

"You're telling me it changed?" he'd said. "The voting age changed?"

She nodded and went back to her meatloaf as though she had mentioned the weather. That night he sat on his bed with his phone and looked it up, and the looking-up was its own strange pleasure, the kind where one answer opens a corridor of other questions. The Twenty-Sixth Amendment set the voting age at eighteen. It was ratified in 1971, and it had gone through in about three months, which the article said made it faster than any other amendment to the Constitution. Faster than any other. He read that sentence twice. Everything he had been taught about American government suggested it was designed to move slowly, glacially, a system of brakes, and yet this one thing had rushed through in a single season of a single year. Why this? Why then? His grandmother had turned nineteen before the country caught up to her.

At school the next day he found Aariz at the bench by the vending machines and told him all of it, the dates, the three months, the comparison. Aariz, who could impugn any statistic within thirty seconds, pulled out his own phone to check.

"About three months," Aariz confirmed, sounding slightly annoyed that there was nothing to dismantle. "Faster than any other amendment. Huh."

"Doesn't that seem backwards to you?" Logan said. "The whole thing is built to be slow. Then everyone suddenly agrees on this one thing and it just, happens."

Aariz shrugged. "Maybe they were embarrassed. Old enough to get drafted, not old enough to vote. That would bother people."

"Nobody's that consistent," Logan said, though privately he wondered whether consistency was even the right measure. Maybe a country could hold two ideas for decades and then, for reasons no one could fully name, simply stop holding one of them.

The gymnasium smelled of floor wax and burnt coffee. Logan carried his ballot to a booth whose privacy curtain no longer reached the bottom, so that he could see Dave from econ class two booths over, hunched like a man defusing something. Logan looked down at his own paper. He had researched the candidates. He had read the local paper's endorsements and then, distrusting the endorsements, gone and found the opponents' own websites, which mostly impugned each other's records in language so loaded it was nearly useless. He had constructed, over two weeks, a kind of mental spreadsheet, and the spreadsheet kept coming out close. One candidate had experience; the other had proposals Logan actually liked and no evidence he could execute any of them. His mother called this cynicism. Logan thought of it as arithmetic.

He filled in the first circles quickly and then arrived at the race where his spreadsheet had never resolved, state representative, and stopped. He thought about his grandmother again, nineteen years old, newly allowed, standing in some hall like this one in 1971, presumably with the same paper and the same uncertainty, except that her uncertainty had maybe been simpler, a question of whether the new right was real. His was different. He had the right and now had to do something with it, and the two perspectives in his head, the one that said experience mattered and the one that said ideas mattered, refused to merge into a single clear position. He tried imagining explaining his choice to Aariz, then to his grandmother, and noticed the answer changed depending on the listener, which seemed like bad news for the idea that he had an answer at all.

An election worker, the one Ms. González from down the street, he realized, the woman who had campaigned for the library levy and once returned his runaway dog, passed behind him and said quietly, "Take your time, honey. It's not a race." The putative deadline was fictional anyway; the polls were open for hours. He breathed out. Somewhere in the middle of not deciding, he noticed he was deciding, that one column of his mind had quietly begun to outweigh the other, not by argument but by something more like inclination, and he circled a name, feeling both that he had reasoned his way there and that he could not fully reconstruct the route. He decided that was allowed. The amendment itself had gone from nothing to ratified in about three months; presumably whoever voted for it also could not have explained every step.

At the scanner he fed the sheet in and watched it vanish with a mechanical gulp that seemed too small for the occasion. The machine display said his ballot was accepted, and a sticker was pressed into his palm, the round I VOTED one, which he had seen on strangers his whole life without ever considering that it was a thing you received rather than a thing that just existed. He stuck it on his jacket. Outside the hall, Dave was waiting on the steps, bouncing on his heels.

"Who'd you go for, state rep?" Dave asked.

"Not telling," Logan said, and found he meant it, and liked meaning it.

"Seriously? I'll tell you mine."

Logan looked at the parking lot, at the afternoon light going amber on the cars of people still inside, and said, "Buy me a coffee and I'll think about it."

activity: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
knowledge_domain: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
fact: Integrating a velocity function over a time interval gives the displacement, which is the area under the velocity-time graph.
story:
The screen door banged behind Kayla, and the smell of her grandmother's coffee, strong enough to strip paint, met her at the threshold. She spread her calculus homework across the kitchen table between a bowl of green tomatoes and a jar of buttons, and frowned at the page. Draw the region, shade the area under the curve, evaluate the integral. The textbook made it look like a recipe for something she had never tasted. She understood the notation, could follow the rules like steps in a dance, but she could not have said what the answer meant if someone held a gun to her head. Her algebra, atrophied over a summer of nothing but lifeguarding and reruns, wasn't helping either.

"Grandma," she called, "can I ask you something weird?"

Her grandmother came in from the garden with mud on her knees and read the problem over Kayla's shoulder. "We didn't have that when I was in school. We had logarithms and no calculators, and we liked it." She tapped the shaded region with one soil-dark finger. "What's it for, though? Somebody invented it to do something."

"That's the thing. I don't know. It just says area under a curve, but it's a velocity curve, so why would anyone want the area? Areas are for floors and pizza."

Her grandmother laughed and started slicing tomatoes for supper. Outside, the creek ran high and turbid after three days of rain, churning brown past the fence line. "Your grandfather used to say you should always know what a number is standing for," she said. "He'd sit right there and ask me what a dollar was worth until I wanted to throw a spoon at him."

When I drove Kayla into town that evening for her mother's shift change, I noticed she had her notebook open on her lap and her watch in her hand. She didn't explain, and I didn't ask. The summer I turned seventeen, I kept a log of every egg the hens laid for no reason my mother could determine, so I understood the impulse to count things. At the edge of town she said, "Sixty-two," wrote something down, and kept her eyes on the speedometer like it owed her money. This happened the whole way, a number every minute, murmured under her breath. I confess I started driving more smoothly than usual, as if her arithmetic might catch me at something.

Back at the house, after the dishes, she spread the numbers across the table and looked at them a long time. Each minute had a speed attached to it, and the speeds climbed and fell like the creek's banks. She drew a graph, minutes along the bottom, speeds up the side, and plotted her points, and there it was: a curve. Her curve, from my truck. Then she did something strange. She connected the points and started drawing rectangles underneath them, each one minute wide, each one as tall as the speed at that minute. Sixty-two miles per hour for one minute was a rectangle. Fifty-five was a narrower sky. She added the rectangles up, quick arithmetic she did partly in her head, and got a number of miles. I watched her check it against the trip odometer I'd reset in the driveway, and the numbers were close, close enough that she sat back like a person who has picked a lock.

"Grandma," she said. "It's distance. The area under a velocity graph is distance. Actual miles." She was talking fast now, pointing at the rectangles. "Every rectangle is speed times time, and that's a little piece of distance, and the integral is all the little pieces added up. Integrating the velocity over the time interval gives the displacement. That's the area under the curve. That's what the textbook was trying to say and couldn't."

"It's like knowing where you've been," I said, "by looking down at your feet the whole way."

"Not exactly where. It can be off if I only sampled every minute. If I'd read it every second, it'd be closer. Every tenth of a second, closer still." She chewed the end of her pencil. "It never gets perfect, does it? It just gets better." She looked out the window at the creek, still brown and fast in the dusk. "I like that. That it's an answer that admits it's an estimate."

I told her about the farm, then, how it would pass whole to her uncle Roy under my husband's stubborn notion of primogeniture, regardless of who had actually wanted it, and she nodded without taking her eyes off her graph. Later, when I came down for water, the kitchen light was still on and she was asleep in the chair, the pencil still in her hand, her rectangles marching across the page like a fence built to hold something that kept moving.

activity: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
knowledge_domain: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
fact: In The Old Regime and the Revolution, published in 1856, Alexis de Tocqueville argued the Revolution continued the centralization of power already begun under the French monarchy.
story:
Caleb had promised himself he would finish the historiographical essay before the weekend, and it was already Thursday afternoon, and he was still on his first paragraph. Ms. Tehrani had assigned the topic in September: how views of the French Revolution had changed since 1800. He had the books spread across two tables in the school library, Carlyle and Tocqueville and a paperback with a cracked spine called Citizens, and none of them seemed to agree with any of the others.

The problem was not that he lacked sources. The problem was that every historian acted as though the Revolution had a fixed meaning and everyone else had simply gotten it wrong. Carlyle wrote about it like a biblical flood. Others wrote about it like a court case. Caleb could not figure out how to put them in one essay without the essay turning into a list, and Ms. Tehrani had already written "this is a list" at the bottom of his outline in green pen.

Emilee dropped her bag on the chair across from him and stole an orange from his lunch container without asking. She was writing about the Reign of Terror for the same class, and she claimed she had a thesis, which Caleb doubted.

"Read me your first sentence," she said, peeling the orange in one long strip, which was a thing she could do and he could not.

"'The French Revolution has been understood differently by every generation that has written about it.'"

"That's a list sentence."

"I know."

"You need to catch someone doing history, not just summarize them." She pushed a book across the table, the fat beige one he had been avoiding because it was from 1856 and the print was small. "You put this on reserve and you haven't opened it. I saw the slip."

The book was The Old Regime and the Revolution, by Alexis de Tocqueville. Caleb had checked it out because Ms. Tehrani's assignment sheet mentioned it as a turning point, and because it was the only primary historian he could use without reading French. He had carried it around for four days and read the introduction twice and understood none of it. He opened it now to the middle, where a previous student had left a pencil mark in the margin, and began actually reading.

What he found there stopped him. Tocqueville was not writing about the Revolution as a break with the past at all. In The Old Regime and the Revolution, published in 1856, Tocqueville argued the Revolution continued the centralization of power already begun under the French monarchy. Caleb read the passage twice, then a third time, then flipped back to see if he had missed something. He looked up at Emilee.

"That's weird," he said.

"What's weird?"

"The Revolution kept doing what the kings were already doing. Tocqueville says the monarchy started centralizing power and the Revolution just continued it. It's in this chapter. He's saying they overthrew the king and then did the king's work."

Emilee stopped chewing. "Wait. So the thing everyone calls the beginning of modern freedom is a continuation?"

"That's his argument. Published in 1856."

She pulled the book toward her and read the marked page herself, frowning, turning back a leaf and then forward again. "Okay, that actually helps me, because I've been trying to figure out why the Terror looks so much like what came before it. Everyone keeps telling me it's the Revolution going wrong. What if it's not a detour?"

"It's more like the same road," Caleb said, and then, because it sounded too neat, "or he thinks it's the same road. I don't know if it's true."

"That's the essay, though." She slid the book back. "That's your whole essay. Everyone before him treats 1789 as year zero, and he comes along in 1856 and says nothing broke. Then you show what everyone after him did with that."

Caleb sat for a moment with his pen not moving. It felt like the first real thought he had had about the topic in three weeks, and it also felt borrowed, because it was Tocqueville's thought, and because Emilee had handed him the shape of the essay in one sentence. He tried to contextualize it, the way Ms. Tehrani kept telling them to: who was Tocqueville writing for, what had happened in France by 1856 that made a man look backward instead of forward. He wrote two sentences about that and stopped again.

"It's not enough to say he disagreed," Caleb said. "The assignment's about how views changed. I need the before and the after, and I only have the middle."

"So get the before. It's Carlyle, he's on your table, he's basically the before." Emilee stood, gathered her orange peel into her palm, and paused. "The after is harder. I read somewhere that people either loved Tocqueville's book or hated it, and the people who hated it still had to answer him."

Miah arrived at the table twenty minutes later with two coffees he was not supposed to have in the library, set one in front of Caleb without comment, and asked what they were doing. Caleb explained, working it out as he spoke, that his essay could not be a list of historians if each one was responding to the last, that disagreement itself could be the subject. Miah listened with the melancholic patience of someone who had finished his own draft on Tuesday.

"So what do you actually think?" Miah asked. "About whether he's right. You can't write nine pages of other people arguing without landing somewhere."

"I don't know yet," Caleb said. He tapped the beige book. "The kings were already centralizing, so the Revolution continuing it fits. But fitting isn't the same as being right, and I haven't read enough to know what the counterargument even is." He pulled a clean sheet of paper toward him and wrote at the top, in handwriting that was going to be a problem later: Thesis: historians after 1856 could not avoid Tocqueville. Then, underneath: What I still don't know.

He underlined the second line twice, and opened Carlyle.

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: The square graduation cap is called a mortarboard because it resembles the flat board bricklayers use to hold mortar.
story:
The gymnasium smelled of floor wax and somebody's mother's perfume, and Antoine's cap kept sliding off the back of his head like it had somewhere better to be. He grabbed it as it fell for the third time and stood in the line of graduates near the stage, where Mr. Ahmed was taping down a curl of banner that read CONGRATULATIONS, CLASS OF 2025.

"Why is it shaped like this?" Antoine said, holding the thing out to Dalton, who was next to him flipping through the program looking for his own name. "It's a square on your head. Whoever designed this hated us."

"I don't know, ask the wind," Dalton said. He didn't look up. Dalton had a scholarship to a university four provinces away and had spent the last two weeks talking about it the way people talk about weather they can't change.

Antoine turned the cap over in his hands, ran his thumb along the flat top, and stopped. The board was stiff and flat, like something a workman would carry. He'd spent two summers helping his uncle lay a patio, and he recognized the shape before he could name it. "It's like the board bricklayers use," he said slowly. "To hold the mortar. My uncle has one. Exactly this shape."

Felix-Antoine, in front of him in the line, twisted around. He was the only person in the class who'd been calling Antoine "the other one" since grade ten, and by now it was almost a term of affection. "What are you on about?"

"It's called a mortarboard," Antoine said. "Because it looks like the board bricklayers use to hold mortar." He had never actually heard anyone say the word before; it arrived in his mouth fully formed, the way things you half-learned do.

"That's the dumbest thing I've heard all year," Felix-Antoine said, but he took his own cap off and looked at it, and after a moment he laughed, a short surprised sound. "We're all wearing little trays of cement."

Mr. Ahmed clapped his hands then and told them it was five minutes, that the doors would open and the parents would come in and anyone not in alphabetical order would answer to him. The line shuffled and sorted itself. Antoine found his place between Felix-Antoine and a girl whose name came alphabetically after his, and his cap slid off again, and he held it against his chest.

The thing he hadn't told anyone was that he wasn't going to the university that had accepted him. Two weeks ago the tuition letter had come with the number his mother would have to cover after the loans, and he'd spent the time since then doing the arithmetic of it in the margins of his notebooks, and last Tuesday he'd signed the deferral form. A year working for his uncle, laying stone, and then maybe. Or maybe the year would become two, the way years did. He had two ways of thinking about it and he could not make them agree: one said that staying was practical, that the money was real, that plenty of people began late; the other said that late was a word the world used to disenfranchise people like him quietly, without ever saying no outright.

The doors opened and the noise of the crowd came in like weather. Dalton's parents were somewhere in the third row; Antoine's mother was by the far wall because she'd come straight from her shift and hadn't wanted to be seen in her uniform. She caught his eye and raised one hand, not waving, just lifting it, the way you'd hold up a lantern.

In biology they'd spent a month on speciation, on how a population separated by a river or a highway becomes, over enough time, something that can no longer cross back. Felix-Antoine had loved that unit. "It's the same with people," he'd said at the time, and Antoine had argued with him, because he believed then that people chose, that a river was only water. Now he was less sure. He looked down the line at the eighty caps, the square boards balanced on eighty heads, and thought about how some of them would cross the river and some would stay on this side, and how five years from now the difference would not seem like a difference at all to anyone standing in this gym, and would seem like everything to the ones wearing it.

Mr. Ahmed was calling the first names. Dalton would be called early, and Antoine could see him composing his face, pulling his collar straight, doing the small ritual of a person about to become someone with a diploma. Antoine put his cap back on his head. It sat crooked, the tassel hanging over his left ear, and he let it. His uncle's mortarboard, he remembered, had a worn wooden handle, and the mortar on it had hardened in the sun one July afternoon and his uncle had scraped it off with the edge of a trowel and started again without complaint.

"Antoine," Felix-Antoine said suddenly, without turning around, "next year, when I'm doing my lab reports and you're doing whatever you're doing, send me a picture of something."

"Of what?"

"Anything. Whatever you see that day."

Antoine's name was called, or nearly called; Mr. Ahmed paused over it, the way he always did, as though checking some private register of who deserved the full four syllables. Antoine stepped out of the line, one hand flat against the sliding cap, and crossed the floor toward the stage.

activity: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
knowledge_domain: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
fact: In the United States, a conventional mortgage with a down payment below 20 percent usually requires private mortgage insurance, which protects the lender, not the buyer.
story:
The listings had begun to blur together. Kayla had been at her mother's desk for two hours, tabbing between apartment sites, and every unit near campus seemed designed by someone who had never had to pay for one. Eight hundred a month for a studio with a hotplate. Twelve hundred for a place that called a converted closet a second bedroom. Each listing wanted first month's rent, last month's rent, and a security deposit, which meant that even a cheap apartment cost three times its monthly rent just to walk in the door. She opened a spreadsheet and made the columns herself: rent, deposit, bus pass, groceries, the paycheck from the bookstore where she'd been hired for the summer. The numbers did what numbers did.

Downstairs, her grandmother was on the phone with Kayla's older cousin Tanya, and the conversation had grown loud enough to climb the stairwell. Kayla heard the word house, then the word payment, and against her own peevish instinct to shut the door, she left it open. Tanya was twenty-five, the one the whole family lionized at every reunion, the first to buy property, the one whose closing had been photographed like a graduation. If Tanya was explaining money, Kayla wanted it.

"It's on the statement every month," her grandmother said, cradling the phone against her shoulder while she washed lettuce. "A separate charge. Forty-something dollars."

Kayla came down halfway and sat on the stairs, notebook in her lap, pretending to look something up on her phone.

"Tell her what the man at the bank called it," her grandmother said, holding the phone out toward the stairwell. "Kayla, you should hear this. You're going to be doing all this soon enough."

"Private mortgage insurance," Tanya's voice said, tinny but clear. "Because we only put ten percent down. Under twenty percent, you have to carry it."

"And here's the part that gets me," her grandmother said, taking the phone back. "Tell her who it protects."

"The lender," Tanya said. "Not us. We pay for it every month and it does nothing for us at all."

"Nothing," her grandmother repeated, snapping a towel against the counter. "The bank gets covered and we get the bill."

Kayla wrote it down, the whole shape of it, in the shorthand she used for things she suspected she'd need: mortgage means you borrow; down payment is the part you pay up front; under twenty percent down, there's private mortgage insurance, and it protects the lender, not the buyer. She sat with the pen stopped against the page. Twenty percent of even a cheap house was an impossible sum, the kind of money that took a decade, and yet the family had thrown Tanya a party. Ten percent down had still been enough to make everyone cry at the photos.

She went back up and opened a new tab. She typed the difference between renting and buying, then a mortgage calculator, then, when the calculator demanded numbers she didn't have, she stopped and just looked at the screen. The cursor blinked in the empty field where a home price should go. Behind every listing she'd scrolled through that morning was this other system, the one Tanya had entered, with its insurance that cost money and covered someone else. Renting felt, suddenly, less like throwing money away and more like paying for the right to leave. Buying felt less like arriving and more like standing at the start of a very long corridor with a charge attached to every month of it.

It was the phone call from her mother that rearranged everything, and Kayla hadn't known it was coming, which was the point of the call. Her mother had been in the apartment over the laundromat for eleven years, and the building had been sold in March, and the new owner wanted everyone out by September. She had a chance at a small house on the west side, her mother said, the first one she'd ever looked at seriously, and the bank had preapproved her, and there was just this one fee on the estimate she didn't understand. She'd texted a photograph of it. Could Kayla, who was good with computers, look it up?

Kayla opened the photo. At the bottom of the loan estimate, in the monthly payment breakdown, under principal and interest and property tax, was a line labeled PMI, and an amount. She recognized it before she finished reading, and something in her chest went tight and strange, the feeling of having learned a thing two hours before it was needed.

She called Tanya back herself. "The number they gave my mom," she said. "Does the insurance come off later, once you've paid enough?"

"It can," Tanya said. "Once you get to twenty percent equity. But that's years for us. Maybe five."

Her mother came home at six with a folder from the bank and stood in the kitchen not opening it, the way she stood when she was deciding whether a thing was good news or a trap. Kayla carried her laptop down and set it on the counter beside the folder. She turned the screen so her mother could see the spreadsheet, the columns she'd built for an apartment she might not need now, and then the other tab, still open, with the calculator and its blinking cursor.

"It's called private mortgage insurance," Kayla said. "I know what it is. I found out today."

Her mother looked at the folder, then at the screen, then at her. "How much do we actually have," she said, "if we put it all down at once?"

Kayla pulled out the chair and sat, and started typing.

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
knowledge_domain: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
fact: In Pride and Prejudice, the Bennet estate is entailed to a male heir, Mr Collins, so none of the five Bennet daughters can inherit their father's home.
story:
Mr Sok had written two questions on the board before Vincent even sat down: Who owns the house, and who is allowed to want things? Below them, the words Marxist lens and feminist lens, and under those, a photocopied page from Pride and Prejudice, the scene where Mr Collins proposes to Elizabeth. Vincent had read the chapter twice the night before and underlined nothing, because he could not decide what mattered. Around him the seminar tables had been pushed into a circle, and Vivian was already flipping through her annotations with the concentration of someone who intended to speak first and last.

"We should start with Collins," she said, when Mr Sok opened the floor. "He's absurd. The whole proposal is absurd. He talks about marriage like a business memo." She read a line aloud, the one about being uniformly consistent in his attentions, and a few people laughed.

Vincent looked at his copy. He had laughed too, the first time. This morning on the bus he had tried the exercise Mr Sok had assigned, reading the same page once for gender and once for class, and the two readings had not lined up. In one, Collins was a fool insulting a clever woman. In the other, the fool was doing arithmetic, and the arithmetic was sound.

Ophelia raised her hand partway, which for her was a demand. "I don't think the marriage plot is the frame. I think the property is." She turned to Vincent, suddenly, as if she had seen him arrive at the same place and wanted backup. "Tell them what you told me in the hall."

He hadn't told her much, only a sentence, but the room waited. "The estate is entailed," Vincent said. "It passes to a male heir. Mr Collins inherits it, so none of the five Bennet daughters can inherit their father's home." He heard the sentence land differently than it had in the hallway, harder, because there were witnesses. "It's in the book. Their home goes to a cousin they can't stand, and when their father dies they're out."

Vivian sat back. "So Mrs Bennet's matchmaking, the nerves, the whole performance."

"Makes sense," Ophelia said. "Five daughters, no inheritance, one house about to leave the family. Her panic is strategy with bad manners."

"That's a Marxist reading," said a boy across the circle. "Or is it feminist?"

"That's the problem," Vincent said, before he could soften it. He had been circling this since the bus. "They're not modular. You can't pull them apart and use one at a time. Elizabeth's refusal only means something because she's refusing money she needs. If she were rich, saying no would cost her nothing. If she were a son, nobody would be asking her to say yes." He was talking faster than he meant to. "The lens I actually want is whatever sees both at once, and I don't think it has a name on the board."

Mr Sok, who had been standing near the window with his arms folded, said only, "Keep going," which was his way of saying he agreed or disagreed or neither.

Vivian was quiet for a moment, marking her page. Then she said, "Fine, but the entail doesn't excuse everything. Darcy's first proposal is still insulting. Money doesn't make him condescending."

"Nobody said it did." Vincent checked his own tone and lowered it. "I'm not ascribing virtue to anyone because they're poor. I'm saying the system sets the prices and the people improvise. Elizabeth improvises better than most."

"Trenchant," said Ophelia, almost smiling. "Also, you stole my thesis."

"Your thesis was about Mrs Bennet. I'm keeping that part."

Mr Sok walked to the board and drew a single line connecting his two questions, then wrote beneath them: so what does the novel call love? He told them to write for five minutes and pass it to the left. Vincent wrote that he could defend the combined reading on property and gender as far as the entail and no farther, that he could not tell whether Austen believed her happy endings or only priced them accurately, and that this was the part he would not resolve by Friday, when the essay was due.

The papers came back to him folded once, the way Vivian handed everything over, as though it were a document in a transaction. He opened it. At the bottom of her page, in the margin, she had written: Collins still absurd. But I read the entail twice. He looked up; she was watching him, pen already moving on a fresh sheet.

activity: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
knowledge_domain: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
fact: Air resistance slows real projectiles, so a thrown ball usually lands shorter than the calculation that ignores air resistance predicts.
story:
The competition rules were taped to the front bench of the lab: each team got three launches, a spring launcher clamped at a fixed angle, and a paper target on the floor. Ms. Joseph had approved the event and then sat at the back with a thermos, refusing to coach anyone. Maelle read the rules twice, copied the launcher's angle into her notebook, and began separating the launch speed into its horizontal and vertical parts, because that was the method she had spent two weeks learning and she intended to use it in front of judges who would ask questions afterward.

Sahar measured the height of the launcher's mouth above the floor with a metre stick and wrote it down. Landon was put in charge of the stopwatch, though he kept flicking it open and shut like a detective in a film he'd seen. Maelle did the arithmetic in blue pen. The vertical component decided how long the ball would stay in the air; the horizontal component, which stayed constant through the whole flight, decided how far it would travel in that time. She multiplied the two together and got a landing distance, and the three of them paced it out from the muzzle and set the target there, fixing it to the tile with four pieces of tape.

The judges arrived at eleven: two graduate students with clipboards and a laminated score sheet. The first team launched and missed by half a metre, which made Landon unreasonably confident. Maelle recalculated everything while Sahar loaded the spring, and the numbers held. "Point eight six metres from the muzzle," she said, and Sahar tapped the target's centre with her toe.

The ball rose, arced, came down, and struck the floor a full hand-span short of the target's near edge. It bounced once and rolled into the leg of the adjacent bench. Landon said a word he shouldn't have, and one of the judges wrote something. Sahar picked up the ball and put it in Maelle's palm without a comment, which was worse than a comment.

The judges allowed the teams to adjust between launches, so Maelle had about six minutes. She checked the arithmetic first, line by line, expecting a slipped digit. There was none. She checked the angle, the height, the value they'd used for the launch speed, which they had measured themselves the week before by firing the ball straight up and timing it. All of it was faithful. She sat with the pen uncapped and watched the second team's ball fall short too, and then the third team's, each one landing inside its own target's shadow but never on the paper, and she began to suspect the problem was not in anyone's arithmetic.

"Your method is right," one of the judges said, walking past, "but ask yourself what the equations ignore." He moved on before she could answer, which she suspected was a rule of the event, or possibly of judges generally.

She wrote "ignore" in the margin and looked at it. The whole method treated the ball as though nothing touched it between the muzzle and the floor, as though the air were not there at all. But the air was there; she could feel the draught from the window on her wrist. She thought of the football she'd kicked in the park last summer, how it had seemed to sag early whenever she put any loft on it. She said it out loud, slowly, testing it. "Air resistance slows real projectiles. So the ball lands shorter than the calculation says."

Sahar leaned over the notebook. "Shorter every time?"

"Every time," Maelle said. "That's why everyone's missing in the same direction. Nobody's over-shooting." She looked at the target, still taped where the clean calculation had put it, and felt the odd double vision of holding two positions at once: the method was correct, and the method was wrong about the world. Both were true, and she could not yet make them one thing. The gap between them was not a mistake she could find and cross out. It was a gap she would have to learn to carry.

They had one launch left. There was no way to calculate the correction exactly, so Maelle did the unscientific thing and slid the target toward the launcher by the width of her hand and a little more, judging from where all three balls had struck. Landon objected that it was a guess. "It's a guess in the right direction," she said. "Staying where we are is a guess too, we just feel safer making it." She pressed the tape down with her thumbnail.

The glacial progress of the judge's pen across the score sheet had been a disincentive to arguing further, so Landon only reloaded the spring. Sahar tried to propitiate the judges with an offer of biscuits from her bag, which they declined with a politeness that achieved nothing. Ms. Joseph, at the back, turned a page of her newspaper and did not look up, though Maelle noticed she had stopped reading it.

The second launch rose, bent, and came down on the edge of the moved target, half on the paper, half on the tile. Sahar shouted. The judge wrote, considered, and said, "Partial credit, and you'll need to tell us why you moved it."

Maelle stood, holding the notebook open to the margin where the word "ignore" sat, and said, "I can do that."

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: Holding static stretches for a long time, about 60 seconds or more per muscle, right before explosive activity can briefly reduce strength and power, so many programs warm up with dynamic movement.
story:
Ava taped the blank grid to the inside of her locker door on Monday morning, seven columns, one for each day until Saturday's time trial. The coach had said, in the flat voice she used for ultimatums, that anyone who wanted a spot on the relay squad had to submit a written weekly plan by Friday, and that "rest" had better appear on it as something other than an accident. Ava had never planned a week of training in her life. She ran when she felt like running, which used to be most days, and lately was every day, because the trial was coming and Amna kept improving.

At lunch she spread the grid on the cafeteria table between Amna's elbows and Josh's chemistry textbook. "I put a long stretching session right before each hard session," she said, tapping Wednesday's box. "An hour of holds. That's what my club coach used to make us do before races."

"Before races," Amna said. She didn't look up from her sandwich.

"Static stuff. The kind where you hold a stretch and count."

"I know what static means," Amna said. "I'm asking when."

Josh pulled the grid toward him and squinted at it. "Wednesday says tempo run, six by four hundred. That's an explosive session, basically."

"It's fast, so I loosen up first. Obviously."

He slid the grid back. "My brother's sprint coach yells at people for exactly that. Some guy on his team used to hold long stretches on the start line and then feel flat in the race. Like he'd spent his strength before the gun." Josh went back to his homework, already bored, and the conversation might have died there except that Amna turned fully around in her seat.

"How long were the holds?"

"Sixty seconds a muscle, something like that," Ava said. "You breathe into it. It's supposed to be the disciplined way."

Amna wiped her hands on a napkin. "So write it down. Sixty seconds or more, per muscle, right before explosive work. Then look at it tonight and tell me if you still believe it."

The afternoon had that late-September smell of cut grass and cold metal bleachers. Ava ran her easy miles, and while she ran she kept arranging the week in her head the way she arranged it on paper: hard days stacked, no gap, the plan a kind of proof of seriousness. She had once overheard an older girl in the change room call her a dilettante, and the word had ionized something in her, split a vague wanting into charged halves: the part that trained and the part that merely admired people who trained. A plan was supposed to settle the question. But Josh's story had lodged sideways, and by the time she reached the track fence she had stopped trusting her own grid.

That evening she sat on her bedroom floor with her laptop and her notes from the season. Two Saturdays ago, before the invitational, she had done her long stretch routine in the infield, holding each hamstring stretch past a minute, feeling virtuous and loose. She'd run her worst 400 of the year, heavy-legged off every curve, and blamed the wind. She found the race in her log. Then she found an older meet, one where she'd only jogged and done dynamic drills, leg swings and walking lunges and skipping, and she'd run a personal best on legs that had felt springy and light. She sat with the two pages side by side for a long time, the desk lamp humming, her knee aching faintly where she'd been pressing it into the carpet.

Thursday after school she found Ms. Harper in the empty gym office, marking with the door open, and asked if she could borrow the whiteboard markers. Ms. Harper looked at the grid under Ava's arm, then at her face, and handed over the whole cup without a word, which Ava appreciated more than any speech. She taped the grid to the gym wall and rebuilt it in front of Amna, who had come to shoot free throws and instead stood holding the ball on her hip.

"Here's what I think happens," Ava said, drawing arrows. "Long holds, sixty seconds or more per muscle, right before explosive work, can briefly reduce your strength and power. It's temporary, but a race is exactly the wrong moment to be temporarily weaker." She tapped Monday through Saturday with the marker. "So the hard days stay, but the long static work moves to the end of sessions, after we've run, or to the evening when it doesn't matter. Beforehand: dynamic movement. Leg swings, lunges, skips. Short, moving, warm."

"And Sunday?" Amna said.

"Rest. Actual rest, written in pen." Ava hesitated, marker uncapped, because the honest part was coming and she could feel it. "The thing is, I don't know where the line is. Whether a thirty-second hold is fine, whether it's only power that drops and not endurance, whether it's the same for everyone. I'm going with dynamic before, long holds after, because my own two races point that way and because it costs me nothing to warm up moving. But it's still a bet."

Amna bounced the ball twice, caught it. "Better than a guess dressed up as a plan."

Friday morning Ava slid the finished sheet under the coach's office door before first period, seven days inked, rest day defended in a margin note, the dynamic warm-up circled in blue. At afternoon practice the coach read it standing on the infield, wind flipping the corner of the page, and Ava watched her eyes travel down the columns and stop, twice, on the blue circles. The coach looked up across forty meters of grass and held the paper out toward her.

"Saturday, you lead the warm-up," she called. "Everyone skips your old routine."

Ava jogged out to the first cone, the frost not yet off the white lines, and started swinging her leg against the goalpost.

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: Elgar took the title Pomp and Circumstance from Shakespeare's Othello, which mentions the "pride, pomp, and circumstance of glorious war."
story:
The folding chairs had been laid out on the football field with a geometry so exact that Cole suspected the vice principal had personally delimited each row with a tape measure, and somehow his chair, third from the aisle in the G section, felt like both a prize and a cage. He was graduating in forty minutes. He was also, according to the program folded into his palm, giving the student address in twenty-five, and the speech in his blazer pocket was not the speech he wanted to give.

He'd written two. The first one, the one in his pocket, had been workshopped by a committee of adults who described it as "mature" and "unifying," which in the vernacular of school administrators meant it said nothing in particular with excellent posture. The second one lived only in his head, and every time he rehearsed it silently it got bigger and less safe.

The band started playing the processional. Cole stood, tugged his gown straight, and fell into the slow march behind Margaret, who had the M's two rows ahead of him and a red tassel that she'd sworn she'd dye and then actually done, which was the most Margaret thing possible.

"Pomp and Circumstance," she said over her shoulder, not quite humming it. "You know where the name comes from?"

"Elgar," Cole said, because that much had been drilled into them by the band director since freshman year. "Elgar wrote it."

"Elgar took the title from Shakespeare. Othello. There's a line in the play about the pride, pomp, and circumstance of glorious war." She said it lightly, the way she quoted everything, as though the words were slightly funny and slightly sad at once. "We read it in English this spring. You were in the other section."

"Glorious war," Cole repeated. The brass swelled behind them, and the phrase sat strangely against the melody everyone associated with crying mothers and rented gowns. "So the song we graduate to is named after a phrase describing war."

"A phrase listing what Othello's lost, actually. But sure." She grinned. "Anyway, your speech. Mackenzie says you rewrote it."

"I didn't rewrite it. I just keep not reading the one I have."

"That's not an answer, Cole."

They reached their rows and had to separate, and Cole sat down with the fact turning over in his mind like a coin he couldn't stop flipping. The principal said something about journeys. The salutatorian said something about doors opening, which Cole noted was a metaphor that had never once been examined by anyone, since a door only opens onto whatever is actually behind it, which might be a hallway or a dumpster.

Mr. Fernando, who had coached Cole in debate for three years and who was stationed at the edge of the stage adjusting the microphone with the seriousness of a man defusing something, caught his eye and gave a small nod. Cole had asked him once, back in April, what made a speech good. Mr. Fernando had said, "Say the true thing early, while you're still scared," which was the most sagacious piece of advice Cole had ever received and also the reason he hadn't slept properly in two weeks.

Then his name was in the mouth of the principal, and his legs carried him up the steps, and the program said "Student Address, Cole" and the pocket said one speech and his head said another. He unfolded the committee's version. He looked out at four hundred gowns and a horizon of relatives holding their phones like candles.

"I was going to read this," he said, "but I found out an hour ago that the music we just marched in to, Pomp and Circumstance, Elgar took that title from Shakespeare, from Othello, a line about the pride, pomp, and circumstance of glorious war." He paused. The microphone made a small plastic click, as if it were swallowing. "Which is a strange thing to graduate to. Unless it's the right thing. Because tomorrow most of us lose the version of ourselves that had a building and a bell schedule around it, and whatever we march toward next, we don't get to know yet whether it's glorious or just loud. I'm not going to pretend I know. I'm going to say we get to find out, and that most days that feels like enough, and some days it doesn't, and both of those are allowed."

He talked for two more minutes, less brilliantly than the version in his head but more honestly than the one in his pocket, and when he sat down Margaret turned around in her chair, walking backward through the alphabet with her eyes, and mouthed, "Dumpster doors?"

"Mackenzie told you," he mouthed back.

The diplomas went fast after that, names swallowed by the wind, and when the band struck up the recessional it was, of course, Pomp and Circumstance again, the same song, the war phrase set to the same swelling brass, and Cole stood up and marched out through it grinning at the absurdity of the whole arrangement. His father's phone was already out, filming. Cole waved, diploma in hand, and heard the woman in the folding chair behind him say to her husband, "What a beautiful piece. They should play that at weddings."

activity: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
knowledge_domain: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
fact: In his Poetics, Aristotle said a well-made plot is a whole with a beginning, a middle and an end.
story:
The community theatre smelled of dust and hot glue, and William sat in the third row of folding chairs with his notebook open to a page that had been blank for three days. Ms. Jean-Louis had given them the assignment two weeks ago: a ten-minute play drawn from a moment in their own lives, staged by the end of the month. Everyone else had pages. Tenzin had pages, Cordelia had pages, even the quiet boy from the technical crew had pages, and William had a title he had already crossed out.

"Read yours again," he said to Tenzin, mostly to postpone his own failure.

Tenzin stood, cleared his throat, and performed the argument between his mother and his uncle about the restaurant they co-owned, the receipts, the uncle who wanted to sell. He did both voices. When he finished, he lowered the script and waited, and the silence went on one beat too long, and William realized he was waiting for more.

"That's it?" Cordelia asked from the lighting booth, where she was rigging a spare instrument she had no reason to rig except that she wanted the booth to herself. "What happened with the restaurant?"

"It's still there," Tenzin said. "They still fight. Last week it was about the freezer."

"So nothing changed."

"Everything in my family stays exactly the same."

William looked down at his blank page and felt something shift, the way a lock feels different when you stop forcing it. He had been trying to write about the day his father moved out, and it kept sprawling, because the day had no shape; it began somewhere unmarked and never concluded, it just thinned into weeks of custody schedules. He had assumed that meant it was unstageable. But the problem was not the material. The problem was that he had not yet decided where to delimit it, where to place the edge that turned a stretch of life into a story with walls.

He raised his hand, then felt stupid and lowered it. "Ms. Jean-Louis said something last week," he said instead. "About Aristotle. In his Poetics, he said a well-made plot is a whole with a beginning, a middle and an end."

Tenzin squinted. "A whole."

"A whole. Like, it's complete. It doesn't leak." William was working this out as he spoke, testing it aloud. "Your play starts, and it stops, but stopping isn't ending. An ending is when something changes, or we know it won't."

"So what do I do? Lie? Say they sold it?"

"No. Pick the fight where something did change. Even a small thing." William found himself leaning forward, curious now about Tenzin's family in a way he had never been, curious how the machinery of it worked. "Was there ever a fight where somebody apologized? Where your mother won? Where the freezer got bought anyway?"

Tenzin sat down slowly on the edge of the stage. "There was one," he said. "My cousin recorded it on her phone. My uncle said the word for family in Tibetan and my mother cried and then they laughed at the freezer anyway. I could end it there." He looked almost truculent about it, jaw set, as if admitting the moment existed cost him something. "But that makes it a happy play. It isn't one."

"Doesn't have to be happy," Cordelia called down, adjusting her instrument so its beam hit exactly center stage, where the fight would happen. "It has to be whole."

William wrote at the top of his page: beginning, middle, end. Not the day his father left, then, but the hour before, the drive to the theatre of all places, his father teaching him to parallel park in the empty lot behind it, failing him, laughing, and neither of them saying the word moving. That had a beginning and a middle. Whether it had an end he would only find out by writing toward it, and he suspected the ending would not be the thing he planned but something he overheard on the way, the way he had overheard the shape of Tenzin's play sitting here doing nothing.

"There's a word for this, isn't there," Tenzin said. "For reading your own life like a text."

"Hermeneutics," William said, pleased with himself, then less pleased, because the word was a door he could point at but not yet open. "Ms. Jean-Louis used it once. I think it means interpretation, the study of how you read things. I don't fully get it."

"Then write the play you do get," Cordelia said. "Ten minutes. One lot, one car, one hour before." She brought the spare instrument down from the booth and set it at the edge of the stage, angled low, like a setting sun. "You can have this light for it."

Tenzin picked up his pencil and crossed out his title. William opened his notebook and wrote the first line of dialogue, the one his father had actually said, which was "You're too far from the curb, kid, you're always too far from the curb."

activity: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
knowledge_domain: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
fact: An ad hominem argument attacks the person making a claim instead of the claim itself, and it is treated as a fallacy in formal debate.
story:
The festival had taken over the river park for the weekend, and by noon the whole field smelled like grilled corn and fried dough. Kayla had come for the food and to help Adele at the heritage booths, but she had stopped in front of a long table with a hand-lettered sign in Spanish: Debate de cinco minutos, tema libre. A man behind the table, Mr. Weber from the community college, was explaining the rules in slow, patient Spanish, and Kayla understood maybe two words in three, which felt like more than she had any right to expect after four years of classes and zero conversations.

She wanted to try it. That was the strange part. She had spent her whole senior year avoiding anything where she might be heard failing, and here she was signing her name on a clipboard. Adele appeared at her elbow with a cup of mango and read the sign over her shoulder. "You're going to debate in Spanish," she said, not quite a question. "For five minutes. Out loud." Kayla said yes, and Adele said nothing else, just pulled up a folding chair near the front, which was somehow both a disincentive and a reason to go through with it.

The topic, drawn from a coffee can, was whether the city should make the festival free for everyone or keep charging admission to fund it. Kayla spent her ten minutes of preparation arguing with herself in two languages at once. In English she thought about the booths, the performers, the fact that nobody got paid if nobody paid. In Spanish, slower, she kept circling back to a girl she'd seen outside the gate that morning, counting coins with her mother. Two frameworks, two verdicts, and no clean way to hold both.

Her opponent turned out to be Kellen, a classmate she'd known since eighth grade, who had grown up hearing Spanish from his grandmother and spoke it the way other people breathed. He opened smoothly, laying out the funding argument, and Kayla made herself stand up and answer. Her accent was not subtle. Somewhere in her second sentence, Kellen smiled, and in his third he interrupted her with a remark to the audience about how they were getting a "very special pronunciation" today. People laughed. Her next sentence dissolved.

She sat down with her ears burning and tried to figure out what had just happened, because it wasn't that he'd beaten her point. He hadn't touched it. Her claim about the girl at the gate was still standing there, unanswered, while everyone in the folding chairs chuckled at how she'd said the word puerta. Was that allowed? Was that even an argument? She leaned toward Adele, who was majoring in nothing yet but had done a season of debate club, and Adele whispered, "That's ad hominem. He's attacking you, not the point. It's a fallacy in formal debate, you can call it."

In her next turn Kayla stood, gripped the edge of the table, and said the words she'd just learned, carefully, twice: "Ad hominem." She told the audience, in her lumpy but legible Spanish, that Kellen had attacked her accent instead of answering her question, and that the question was still there. She watched the words land. A woman in the second row nodded. Mr. Weber's pen stopped moving over his clipboard, and then he wrote something down, and Kayla understood that the mock had cost Kellen something real in the scoring, though she couldn't have prognosticated that a minute earlier and wouldn't pretend she could have.

She finished her five minutes. Her Spanish fell apart twice and she rebuilt it in view of everyone, which felt seismic in a small, private way, like a floor tile shifting under her feet. When Mr. Weber called time, Kellen shrugged and said, in English, "Okay, that was actually good," which was not an apology, and Kayla found she didn't need it to be one. What she still didn't know was who was right about the fee, and she said so in her closing: that she believed the gate should be open and the performers deserved their money, and that she had not yet found the argument that proved both could be true at once.

Afterward Adele bought her a churro and they walked past the booths toward the stage where the drummers were setting up. Kellen caught up with them at the edge of the crowd, holding his own coffee can topic slip, and held it out so Kayla could read it. The next round started in fifteen minutes, and it was two against two, and he asked her, in Spanish, whose side she wanted.

activity: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
knowledge_domain: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
fact: The US Telecommunications Act of 1996 eliminated the national cap on radio station ownership, and the number of station owners then fell sharply even as the number of stations grew.
story:
Robert had noticed it on the drive back from his cousin's wedding in Columbus, and it had bothered him for two weeks since. The morning show in Columbus had the same host, the same jingle, even the same running joke about a lost bet, as the morning show in his own town three hours away. He'd asked his father why, and his father had shrugged and said something about companies being big these days, which wasn't an answer, it was a shrug in sentence form. So on Tuesday after last period he went to the newspaper office to look it up, because the office had the one computer with a real internet connection and, more importantly, it had Naomy, who had opinions about everything and cited her sources.

The office was a converted supply closet behind the gym, two desks, a filing cabinet, and a poster of deadlines torn in half and taped back together. Ms. Lewandowski, who supervised the paper without ever seeming to supervise anything, was at the window trying to coax a dying fern back to life. Robert dropped his bag and told Naomy about the radio shows.

"That's syndication," Naomy said. "Hosts record one show, stations buy it."

"No, it wasn't just the show. The traffic report named the same intersections like they were local. It was the same station with a different city stickered on."

Naomy spun her chair to face him. "Okay, now I care."

They started with the Federal Communications Commission's own website, and Robert typed slowly, the way he did when he wanted the search terms to be right rather than fast. What they found first was a law. The Telecommunications Act of 1996, Naomy read aloud, had eliminated the national cap on radio station ownership. Before that, there had been a limit on how many stations one company could own across the whole country, and after, there wasn't. Robert sat back. "So anyone could buy as many as they wanted."

"Anyone with money," Naomy said. "So not us."

The next part took longer, because the numbers came from a trade publication and the formatting was terrible. But there it was. After the cap was gone, the number of station owners fell sharply, even as the number of stations kept growing. Robert read the sentence twice, then copied it into his notebook word for word, which he did when something refused to fit the shape he'd expected. More stations, fewer owners. The words sat on the page like a math problem where the answer was somehow less than either of its parts.

"Same shows in two cities," he said slowly. "Same company owning both."

"Which matters," Naomy said, "because somebody decides what gets covered, and somebody owns the somebody."

Robert had come in wanting a fact, the way you want a key to a door you haven't found yet. Now he had the fact and the door was everywhere. He thought of Ms. Lewandowski's journalism unit in the spring, where she'd called him a polymath, mostly because he'd corrected a date in her lecture, and he'd liked the word without fully believing he'd earned it. A polymath would know what to do with this. Robert only knew that the school board was voting next month on a contract with a company that, he now discovered after twenty more minutes of searching, owned six hundred radio stations and was pitching the district a multimedia partnership, complete with a sponsored news segment in the morning announcements.

"That's a story," Naomy said, tapping the screen. "We run it."

"It's more complicated than that." He pulled the notebook toward him. "The company isn't doing anything illegal. The law changed. They're allowed." He paused, aware that he was arguing against the article he wanted to write. "But allowed isn't the same as good. Six hundred stations can make one decision sound like six hundred decisions." He wrote the number down and then, after a moment, crossed it out, because he hadn't verified it and because he suspected himself of wanting it to be terrible.

"So we're careful," Naomy said. "We say what we know. We say what we don't."

Ms. Lewandowski came over, fern abandoned, drying her hands on her cardigan. She read their notes over Robert's shoulder, said nothing for a long moment, and then said, "You'll need to call the company for comment. Before, not after." Robert nodded, though his stomach tightened at the idea of the phone call, the receptionist, the silence on the line.

He stayed after Naomy left, drafting questions in his diurnal notebook, the everyday one he carried everywhere, separate from the assignments. Who owns the stations you'd partner with. Who decides what the sponsored segment covers. What happens if we cover something you don't like. Outside, the janitor's cart squeaked past the door, and somewhere down the hall a radio was playing, tinny and distant, the same song Robert had heard in Columbus.

He picked up the office phone and started dialing the number printed on the contract proposal.

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
knowledge_domain: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
fact: Higher interest rates pay savers more, so households tend to shift some money from spending into savings, which lowers demand for goods and helps slow price rises.
story:
The folder Ms. Sutherland slid across the counter had a sticky note on it that said "read this before you answer the phones," and Alice, who had been told on her first day that the summer teller job was basically a sinecure, a matter of stamping deposits and smiling, was beginning to understand that Ms. Sutherland did not believe in sinecures. The folder held the branch's new rate sheet. The savings rate had gone up. Alice read the number twice, then a third time, because she had been planning, all June, to buy the phone.

She had the money. That was the thing. Two months of paycheques sat in her own account at this same branch, and the poster in the front window that used to make her feel smug, the one about saving for what matters, now felt like it was addressing her personally. Her old phone worked. It held a charge for most of the day and the crack across the corner had stopped spreading. But the new one had a camera that could take pictures of the moon, Gurleen had shown her the moon pictures, dozens of them, silver and cratered and perfect, and Ireland had said the moon pictures were a marketing scam, which had started a war that lasted the whole of Canada Day weekend.

At lunch Alice sat in the back room with the rate sheet still in her pocket, and Ireland, who worked at the grocery store next door and came over to steal the good chair, asked what was wrong with her.

"Nothing. Did you know they raised the savings rate?"

"How much?"

Alice told her. Ireland whistled and pulled out her own phone, the same cracked model Alice had, and did some arithmetic with her thumb. "So if I leave my money in instead of buying stuff, it earns more now. Like actually more, not point-zero-nothing more."

"That's the whole idea, I think. Higher rates pay savers more." Alice heard herself say it and then heard the second half arrive, slower. "So people move money out of spending and into saving. Less money chasing the same stuff. The bank sent a memo about inflation, it said demand comes down and that helps slow price rises."

"You sound like the memo."

"I ate the memo."

Gurleen arrived at three, coming in from the heat with the moon-picture phone in her hand, and asked Alice if she'd decided. This had been the plan for weeks: Alice buys the phone, Gurleen gets Alice's old one, which is better than Gurleen's truly dead one, and everyone is happy. Alice looked at Gurleen's dead phone, its screen so dimmed it had to be held at an angle, and she could see the moment Gurleen understood, because Gurleen was not slow.

"You're not getting the phone," Gurleen said.

"I haven't decided."
