"You're doing the responsible thing. I can see you doing it. Your face is doing it right now." Gurleen set the dim phone on the counter, carefully, the way you set down something you're trying not to slam. "It's fine. It's smart. It's what my dad would say to do."

Alice rang up a deposit for the woman in line behind Gurleen, an elderly woman who counted out twenties with shaking hands and apologized for the shaking, and Alice said, "Take your time, it's a hot one," and meant it, and the woman smiled at her with real gratitude, and that somehow made the whole afternoon harder. After the woman left, Ms. Sutherland appeared beside her station with two teas and set one down on Alice's side.

"You've read the sheet," Ms. Sutherland said.

"Twice. Three times."

"Customers will ask about it. Some will be pleased. Some will be paying more on their lines of credit and they won't be pleased at all, and you'll be the face they see first." She said it without drama, the way you'd mention weather. "It's a trade-off. The same lever that helps one household hurts another. You don't have to defend it. You just have to know it."

Alice turned that over for the rest of her shift, between deposits and a lost debit card and a man who wanted to argue about a hold on a cheque. It wasn't that the memo was wrong. She could see the whole chain now, could practically instantiate it on the counter: rates up, savers paid more, money shifting from spending to saving, demand easing, prices slowing. She believed it. But Gurleen's face, doing that careful not-slamming set of the phone, was also part of the picture, and the woman with the twenties, and the people with the lines of credit she'd never see. The chain was true and it moved through actual people, and it could be true and still cost her friend a working screen.

When the branch emptied she called Gurleen, who answered on the dim phone, squinting.

"I'm not buying it," Alice said. "I'm putting the money in savings, at the new rate. But listen. I get paid again in August. Two more paycheques, and I'll have enough for the phone and the savings top-up both, if I wait till the end of August. That's five weeks."

"Five weeks of my screen like this."

"I know. Or, and tell me if this is insulting, I could get you the old one now and you'd still get the, no, that's the same money. Sorry. I'm still figuring it out. I've never had to make a decision where being right about the theory didn't settle it."

There was a pause, and then Gurleen laughed, short and surprised. "You should write that down. That's the most honest thing anyone's said to me all summer." Her voice crackled through the bad speaker. "Five weeks. But you're coming to the fireworks Saturday, and you're taking pictures with that cracked thing, so I can see exactly what I'm waiting for."

Alice looked at her phone, at the crack, at the corner where it had stopped.

"Deal," she said. "I'll frame the moon."

activity: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
knowledge_domain: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
fact: In Tinker v. Des Moines (1969), the Supreme Court ruled 7-2 that students do not shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech at the schoolhouse gate.
story:
The elevator at city hall smelled like floor wax and old paper, and Morgan rode it to the third floor holding two legal pads, one for each side of Tinker v. Des Moines. She was the only senior Ms. Esposito had ever assigned to argue both petitioner and respondent before the mock court, an honor Morgan suspected was really a punishment for having told the class, back in September, that debate was easy.

"You look like a gourmand who's been handed two menus and can only order from one," Fatima said, meeting her outside the council chamber, where the folding tables had been arranged into a bench. Fatima was holding a bag of cheese popcorn she had no intention of sharing, which made her a gourmand in appetite only.

"I have to order from both. That's the assignment." Morgan balanced the pads on her knee while the elevator doors closed behind a woman from the water department. "Ms. Esposito says if I can't argue against myself, I don't understand the case."

Izaak arrived late, tie already loosened, carrying the printed opinion with three sticky flags bristling from its edges. "You know what you have to find, right? The line. Every dress-code case that comes after Tinker quotes the same sentence."

Morgan did know, and she had found it that morning at the kitchen table while her mother made toast and pretended not to listen. She had read the 1969 opinion twice, the majority and both dissents, and copied the sentence onto each pad in her own handwriting, as though writing it twice might make it say different things. It refused.

Inside the chamber, Ms. Esposito sat at the center of the bench beside a retired judge whose name tag had flipped backward, and a city clerk who had clearly drawn the short straw. The audience was fifteen students, two parents, and a man waiting for the zoning meeting scheduled after them. Fatima took the back row with her popcorn, an honest gourmand at last, eating slowly to make it last the whole session.

Morgan rose for her first argument, the students' side, and found the sentence waiting for her like a coin she had already pocketed. "In 1969, in Tinker v. Des Moines, the Supreme Court ruled seven to two that students do not shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech at the schoolhouse gate." The clerk looked up. The man with the zoning papers looked up too, which surprised her. She argued that a dress code banning political messages was a pernicious kind of silence, that the school had no evidence of disruption, that the arm band and the T-shirt were cousins if not siblings.

Then she sat down, turned her chair the other way, and argued the opposite. This was the part she had dreaded, not because it was hard but because it was easy. She said schools were not public squares, that the principal must act before disruption rather than after, that a majority of the Court in 1969 had still left room for schools to act, and that a ruling seven to two was not the same as unanimous, that even justices can split. She heard her own voice become fluent and did not entirely like it. When the retired judge asked whether she was prevaricating, she had to stop and think, because the honest answer was no, she meant every word, both sets of them, and that seemed worse.

"It's not prevaricating if I actually believe both," she said finally. "Or if I can't tell which one I believe more."

"That," said the judge, "is the first interesting thing anyone has said in this room today."

Ms. Esposito called a five-minute recess, and Morgan stood in the corridor by the drinking fountain, where the water tasted faintly of pennies, and told Fatima the truth: she had entered the building thinking the case was about speech, and now she thought it was about fear, the school's fear of disruption and the students' fear of being made invisible, and the Court had simply chosen which fear to tolerate. "Seven to two," she said. "Which means two justices read the same record and felt the other fear."

"So which side wins?" Fatima crumpled the empty popcorn bag with ceremony.

"That's the thing. Tinker doesn't tell you who wins the dress-code case. It tells you the schoolhouse gate isn't a border crossing. After that, you still have to argue."

When the session resumed, Morgan declined to give a closing for either side. Instead she asked the bench for permission to give one closing that covered both, and Ms. Esposito, after a glance at the judge, nodded. Morgan stood at the podium with both pads closed, because she no longer needed them, and said that the famous line about rights at the schoolhouse gate was a beginning rather than an ending, that it opened a question it could not answer, and that anyone who quoted it as a verdict had not read the two dissents or felt the worry inside the seven.

The judge deliberated with the clerk for less than a minute, whispered something that made Ms. Esposito press her lips together, and announced that Morgan had won the mock court's highest score in the program's nine-year history, a distinction awarded jointly to her and, in the judge's words, to her opponent.

"Congratulations," said Izaak, shaking her hand with complete solemnity. "You beat yourself."

"Seven to two," said Fatima from the back row.

activity: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
knowledge_domain: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
fact: An authentic cadence, a V chord moving to the I chord, sounds final, which is why melodies usually end their last phrase with it.
story:
The kitchen table had been cleared of everything except the manuscript paper, a pencil with teeth marks near the eraser, and Kaitlyn's laptop open to a video about chord voicings that she had paused at the same frame three times. Sixteen bars. She had wanted sixteen bars since March, when Mr. Korhonen had told the theory class that a melody is a kind of argument, that chord changes were the reasons you gave for each note, and that by June she should hand in something written properly, in standard notation, with no cheating by recording it and calling it done.

She had started four times that afternoon. The first attempt died at bar nine, the second at bar three, and the third she crumpled before finishing bar one because the opening note already sounded like a song she couldn't place, some noxious jingle from a commercial, and she couldn't stand the thought that her first melody might secretly belong to a mattress sale. The fourth attempt was still alive. It undulated through the first eight bars, mostly stepwise, with a leap of a sixth in bar five that she liked more than she could justify, and then it stopped. Bar nine. Blank paper, blank mind.

Her phone buzzed against the table. Grace, from the community centre jazz workshop, had sent a voice memo. Kaitlyn played it and heard Grace's half-laughing voice over the sound of somebody's saxophone in the background. "Ahmad played his thing for the group today and everyone clapped, and I played mine and this guy just nodded and said, 'It doesn't sound finished.' What does that even mean? It has an ending. I ended it." Then, closer to the mic, almost conspiratorial: "Can you come down? Bring your paper stuff."

The centre was fifteen minutes away by bike, and Kaitlyn went, folding the manuscript sheets into her back pocket. In the small room with the upright piano and the folding chairs, Ahmad was at the keyboard picking out his own melody again, the one that had made everyone clap. Grace had hers on her phone, a recording she'd made in her bedroom, and she played it twice while Ahmad listened with his eyes closed, which he did when he was being serious and not when he was being polite.

"It just hangs there," Ahmad said when it ended. "Like you walked out of the room mid-sentence." He turned back to the keyboard and played the last four bars of his own piece, and Kaitlyn heard it plainly: the accompaniment shifted, the fifth chord moving home to the first, and the melody landed on the tonic at the same moment, like a door clicking shut. She asked him what that was called, because she was sure it had a name.

"An authentic cadence," Ahmad said. "The V chord moving to the I chord. That's why melodies usually end their last phrase with it. It sounds final."

Kaitlyn had written the words on the back of her hand before she left the centre, and now, back at the kitchen table with the lamp pulled low and the smell of her mother's onion soup drifting in from the stove, she looked at them and remembered something she hadn't thought about in years. In fourth grade, before her family moved, a neighbour used to play old records through his open window on summer evenings, and she used to wait for the moment near the end of each song when the whole thing seemed to lean forward and settle, a feeling like reaching the bottom stair in the dark. She hadn't known it had a name. She hadn't known it was something a person could choose to do, deliberately, with a pencil, on a page. Her teacher had said melody was an argument, and she'd thought that was just an aphorism, one of those tidy sayings adults used instead of showing you anything, but maybe it was literal: some arguments end because they resolve, and some just stop because the speaker got tired.

She sharpened the pencil and looked at bar nine again. She tried writing a V chord under bars fifteen and sixteen, spelling it out below the staff where Mr. Korhonen wanted the changes notated, and then she had to decide what the melody itself would do over it, and that was harder. The leap of a sixth in bar five wanted, she thought, to be answered somewhere, and she wondered whether the answer belonged before the cadence or inside it, or whether a leap like that was allowed to go unanswered the way some questions in an argument were better left hanging. She hummed bar fifteen, the fifth chord underneath, and felt the pull toward home, the whole page leaning toward that last bar the way the records used to lean. Then she pressed the pencil down and wrote the first note of the ending.

activity: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
knowledge_domain: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
fact: In a minor-key sonata-form movement, the exposition's second theme usually moves to the relative major, such as E-flat major in a movement in C minor.
story:
Nathan set the score on the kitchen table between a bowl of cereal he was no longer eating and his mother's unopened mail, and put his pencil behind his ear the way his piano teacher did. Ms. Doyle had given them the assignment on Friday: take the first movement of the Mozart sonata in C minor, mark the exposition, the development, and the recapitulation, and bring the annotated score to the first seminar of the semester. She had said, almost as a dare, that the students who got the second theme wrong would learn the most from getting it wrong. Nathan had underlined that sentence in his notebook, and now he could not stop wondering whether he was one of them.

He played the opening eight bars on the kitchen table, fingering the notes silently on the wood. C minor, firm and dark, a theme like a hand closing into a fist. Then the music loosened, gathered itself, and somewhere around the double bar it turned warm in a way he had not predicted. He stopped. He hummed the second theme back to himself and put his pencil to the staff. If the first theme was in C minor, the second should be in G major. That was the rule he had carried out of high school theory, the dominant for the second subject, the way tension was supposed to be built. But the notes under his pencil were not in G at all. Three flats. He counted them twice, because counting them once felt like misreading.

He texted Cash, who had taken the same theory class and who answered at eleven in the morning like a person with no commitments. "mozart k457 second theme," Nathan typed. "what key am I looking at." Cash replied with a shrugging emoji and then, a minute later, "i got the cd not the score. bring it tonight?" Nathan said he would, but he did not want to wait until tonight. He wanted to know now, the way you want to check a lock after you have already checked it.

He put the recording on his phone and listened with his eyes on the score, following the second theme as it settled into E-flat major. Not the dominant. The key with the same key signature as C minor, its relative, sitting a third below where he had expected the music to climb a fifth. He sat back and looked at the ceiling. Was Mozart breaking a rule, or was the rule simply narrower than he had thought, a rule about major-key movements and not about these darker ones? He tried to remember whether Ms. Doyle had ever said. She had not, or he had not been listening, and the gap between those two possibilities was, for the moment, equivocal.

Ainsley came by in the afternoon to pick up a book she had left after New Year's, found him at the table with the score, and dropped into the chair across from him. "Is that the Mozart thing? I did it yesterday. Took me forty minutes." She leaned over his markings. "Why do you have a question mark there?" He pointed at the second theme. "It's in E-flat major," he said. "In C minor, the second theme goes to the relative major." She looked at him, then at the page, then said, "That's what I got too, and it's in my brother's old textbook." He felt something loosen in his chest, the way a held breath lets go without your deciding it.

They listened together, and he noticed that once he stopped waiting for G major, the E-flat arrival made its own sense, a brightness that felt earned because it came from the same notes the minor key had been using all along. Still, a question stayed with him, and he let it stay. If the form could bend like this, what else in it was bendable? Where exactly did the development begin, and was that measure he had marked a transition or already the unravelling? He drew a second, lighter line and labeled it with a small "maybe," unwilling to pretend certainty he did not have.

At dinner he explained the whole thing to his mother, who had played clarinet in school and asked good questions even when she could not follow. "So the sad key and the happy key share the same notes," she said, stirring something on the stove. "Different home, same furniture." Nathan laughed and said that was better than anything in his textbook, then caught himself wondering whether it was actually true, or only true in a way that worked for keys and not for people. He decided to leave both possibilities open.

He copied his markings into clean ink before bed, the exposition bounded, the recapitulation returning home with the second theme finally in C major, and at the top of the first page he wrote a question for Ms. Doyle, small enough that only he would read it. He set the score by the door next to his shoes, so he could not leave without it, and turned off the kitchen light. "Forty minutes," he said to the dark. "Right."

activity: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
knowledge_domain: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
fact: A margin of error is expressed in percentage points, not percent: plus or minus 3 points on a 58 percent result means a likely range of 55 to 61 percent.
story:
Lea opened the draft at 9:40 on a Tuesday night, two hours before the student paper went to print, and read the sentence she had written that afternoon with the bright, tired confidence of someone working on four hours of sleep. "In a poll of 400 students, 58 percent support the closed-campus proposal, with a margin of error of 3 percent." It had seemed fine at 3 p.m. At 9:40 it made a small cold knot under her ribs, the way a word repeated too many times suddenly looks misspelled.

The poll was the spine of the whole story. Their principal had floated the closed-campus rule after a string of lunchtime walkouts downtown, and the school board would vote in three weeks. Lea had spent a week chasing numbers instead of quotes, and now she had the town's only survey of student opinion, gathered through a form she and Macy had pushed through lunch tables and team group chats. If the numbers were wrong, the story wasn't just weaker. It could be used. Supporters would say a majority backed it; opponents would eviscerate the methodology in the comments, and the comments always found the soft spot first.

She typed "margin of error percentage points" into the search bar, then deleted it, then typed it again. She hated looking things up after writing them. It felt like checking the stability of a bridge after the caravan had crossed.

The first result was a page about survey methods. She scrolled, chewing the inside of her cheek. Somewhere in the middle of the paragraph she stopped, read it three times, and put her hand over her mouth. A margin of error was expressed in percentage points, not percent. Plus or minus 3 points on a 58 percent result meant a likely range of 55 to 61 percent. Her sentence had said "3 percent," and she had meant, without knowing she meant anything, that the error was 3 percent of 58, a shrink-wrapped little number, under two points. She'd made the poll look nearly three times more precise than it was.

Macy was still online. Lea sent the paragraph and waited, watching the three dots appear and vanish twice, which was Macy deciding how to break something gently.

"Okay so we wrote it wrong," Macy finally sent. "How wrong is wrong?"

Lea pulled the phone off the desk and called her. "Wrong like, it's not 3 percent of anything. It's 3 points. Points. That's the word. The real range is 55 to 61, not 56.5 to 59.5."

"So we were too confident."

"Way too confident." Lea looked at the draft window behind her messages, at her own sentence sitting there like a smile with something in its teeth. "And it matters, because 55 is a thinner majority than 61. The story changes depending on which end you're standing on."

There was a pause, and she could hear Macy's television going in the background, some cop show, a detective reciting recidivism rates at a suspect with the weary certainty of a man who had never once been wrong on camera. "Then fix it," Macy said. "Isn't that the whole job? You find out you're wrong and you fix it before anybody else finds out."

"It's not just the fixing. It's the headline." Lea pulled the draft toward her. The headline said "Most Students Back Closed Campus," and under it, her own byline, and under that, the fate of the next three weeks of school-board comment, where adults would quote her number at each other like scripture. "Most could mean 55. Most could mean 61. Both of those are 'most' and they're not the same most."

She tried three headlines. "Students Lean Toward Closed Campus" sounded affective and mushy, like a mood rather than a measurement, and she deleted it, annoyed at herself for reaching for a soft word to cover a hard problem. "Majority Supports Closed Campus, Poll Shows" was cleaner and worse. She sat with her hands off the keyboard for a minute, listening to the fan of the old computer, and then pulled up Mr. Hu's email from September, the one he sent all his journalism students, subject line "when the numbers move." She'd skimmed it then. She read it now.

"I'm not going to tell you what a poll says," it said, near the end. "I'm going to tell you that a poll never says one thing. It says a range, and your job is to not pretend the range is smaller than it is." She closed the email. That wasn't a headline either, but it was a straightedge she could lay against the ones she had.

She wrote: "Students Favor Closed Campus, Poll Finds, 55 to 61 Percent." Then, underneath, in the body, she rebuilt the sentence the way the methods page showed it was done: 58 percent in favor, plus or minus 3 points. She sent the new draft to Macy, then to Sydney for a proofread, then, after another minute, to Mr. Hu, with a two-line note: "I had the margin of error wrong. This is the fix. Am I still overstating it?"

His reply came in eight minutes, which for Mr. Hu at night was practically instantaneous. "Better. You're honest about the range now, which is more than most professionals manage. One question for tomorrow: is 400 enough students to say 'most'? Not a correction. A question."

Lea read it twice. It wasn't a yes, and it wasn't a no, and she understood that he was leaving it that way on purpose, the way he left most things. She saved the file, and the little saved dot appeared in the tab like a period at the end of a sentence she had finally earned, and she texted Macy: "55 to 61. We print the spread, not the snapshot."

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: Many news stories begin with a dateline naming the city where the story was reported, placed before the first sentence.
story:
The fan above Phoenix's kitchen table wobbled on its lowest setting, stirring the papers just enough that Nicolas had to keep one finger on his article to keep it from sliding toward the sugar bowl. The article was in Khmer, printed from a website his mother had bookmarked years ago and he had never opened until this week. Phoenix's grandmother sat at the far end of the table shelling beans, and Phoenix himself leaned over a chemistry notebook, pretending not to listen.

"Read it again," Phoenix said. "Slower. You swallowed half the consonants."

"Your brain melts at the same rate as my motivation," Nicolas said, but he squared the paper and began. He had chosen the article himself, something about a bridge and a river, because his tutor, Mr. Chea, had said summarising news aloud was the fastest way into a language. "Real sentences," Mr. Chea had said. "Not the sentences in textbooks, which no human has ever said aloud."

The first sentence took him nearly a minute. Somewhere in the third line the print seemed to rearrange itself, the way a word stared at too long breaks into strange shapes, and he felt a somatic drag of tiredness, an actual weight in his shoulders, as if his body had already done a full school day and was filing a complaint. He pushed through to the end, laid the paper down, and looked up.

"Okay," he said. "Summary. There's a bridge, and they're inspecting it, and it's in Thailand."

Phoenix lowered his pen. "Thailand?"

"That's what it said. Bangkok, I think. Somewhere near the beginning."

Phoenix's grandmother said something short, and Phoenix laughed, then translated without being asked. "She says the paper in your hand is Khmer and your mother is from Phnom Penh, so either you're reading a Thai newspaper in Khmer script, or you made something up."

"Option two," Nicolas admitted. He picked the paper back up and stared at the top line, the little cluster of words before the first real sentence, the ones he had skipped because they looked like a heading and headings are furniture, things you walk past. He read them slowly. "Phnom Penh." He read them again. "It says Phnom Penh."

"What says Phnom Penh?"

"The dateline," Nicolas said, and as he said the word he understood he had never actually known what it meant before, only that it existed, the way he knew the names of faraway cities. "Many news stories begin with a dateline naming the city where the story was reported, placed before the first sentence. I skipped it. I read the first sentence and decided the story happened there, and the first sentence was about a bridge over a river, and I have no idea which river."

"So the story is from Phnom Penh," Phoenix said.

"Reported from Phnom Penh. I honestly don't know if the bridge is in Phnom Penh or if that's just where the journalist filed it from. Those might be two different things." He ran his thumb along the top of the page. "I got the country wrong, so I'm not going to guess twice."

Phoenix's grandmother set down a pod and spoke again, longer this time, and Phoenix listened with the particular patience of someone who has to decide how much to translate. "She says when she was young the papers were all one page, and the dateline was the only way to know whether the news was near or far. Also she says you hold your pen like a foreigner, which is a separate problem."

Nicolas laughed, and then, because the table was quiet again and the fan kept its slow rotation, he began the summary a second time, this time from the dateline. "This story was reported from Phnom Penh. It is about a bridge being inspected after something, I can't tell what yet, maybe flooding, maybe just age. The bridge is old. The inspectors are coming." It was not much. It was, at least, true in every part he could verify, and he noticed he trusted it more than the earlier version, which had been longer and confident and wrong about an entire country.

Mr. Chea would ask him tomorrow how it went, and Nicolas could already hear the shape of his own answer, something like: badly, then better. He would say he had learned to read the dateline before the first sentence, and that he still could not say for certain where the bridge stood, only where the story came from, and he had decided that admitting the difference did not augur badly for him. For now he folded the article along its old creases and put it in his pocket, where it sat against his ribs like something worth keeping. Phoenix slid the sugar bowl back toward the center of the table and said, "Same time Thursday. Bring the bridge."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Cutting an onion breaks its cells and releases enzymes that produce syn-propanethial-S-oxide, a vapor that irritates the eyes and makes them tear.
story:
Benjamin set the cutting board on the overturned milk crate beside the camp stove, because the kitchen was being refloored and his father had banished all cooking to the backyard until Thursday. The soup was his idea, vaguely: his mother had left a note on the fridge that read, "Dinner is your problem tonight. There are onions. Do not burn the house down. Love, Mom." He had taken this as both an instruction and a compliment, since she would not have trusted Kolton with a stove, and Kolton was the one now sprawled in the folding chair, narrating.

"You're dicing wrong," Kolton said. "Those are not dice. Those are casualties."

"They're rustic." Benjamin squared off the first onion and cut through it, and within seconds his eyes were streaming, which he pretended was the wind. Kolton laughed at him for a full minute, phlegmatic about everything else in his life but somehow incapable of restraint when a friend wept over a vegetable. It was Kolton, too, who had been there in seventh grade when Benjamin, attempting a birthday cake for his mother, had confused baking soda with baking powder and produced something the family still called The Hockey Puck. That failure had been broadcast to three households; this one, Benjamin hoped, would stay between them and the fence.

Then Jamie arrived, texts having preceded her by ten minutes: "coming over, need to escape my house, is the soup real or theoretical." She came through the side gate carrying her chemistry binder, which she set down like a hostage exchange. "I have a test tomorrow," she said, "and I am going to study at you while you cook."

"Sit," Benjamin said, gesturing at the grass, which was the only remaining furniture.

She picked up the second onion to help, since the soup had reached the stage where everything depended on chopping faster, and after her third cut her eyes went red and the tears came in earnest, sliding down her face while she kept cutting. Kolton leaned forward. "Jamie. Jamie. Are you crying? Is the soup emotionally resonant already?"

"It's the onion," she said, but her voice cracked on it, and Benjamin watched Kolton register the crack and not quite know what to do with it, because teasing someone about a vegetable is safe and teasing them about their actual life is not. Jamie wiped her face with the back of her wrist. "My eyes are just doing a thing. It's chemical. I'm not upset."

Kolton opened his mouth. Benjamin said, "Wait," and then, because he was tired and his own eyes still stung, "Jamie, you have the binder. Is there a reason onions do this, or do they just hate us?"

She flipped it open one-handed, onion juice and all, and found the page. "It's a vapor. Syn-propanethial-S-oxide." She said it flatly, like a password. "Cutting the onion breaks its cells and releases enzymes that produce it, and the vapor gets in your eyes and makes them tear." She looked up, eyes streaming, almost defiant about knowing it. "So it's not crying. It's basically an attack."

Benjamin stood there with the knife in his hand, thinking that this changed something, though he could not have said exactly what. He had spent the afternoon predicated on the assumption that the dinner would be the hard part, the thing requiring his competence, and the actual difficulty had turned out to be this: two friends in his backyard, one of whom was crying for a reason and crying for the onion at the same time, and no way to tell the two apart. He thought of his mother's note again, the small encapsulation of her trust in him, the whole message compressed into "your problem tonight," and understood that she had not meant the soup.

"Jamie," he said. "Is the test the thing, or is the test a smaller thing next to a bigger thing?"

"The test is fine. The house is loud. My dad's on the phone all night about the job." She went back to the onion, slicing with more force than the recipe required, and the tears kept coming, and Kolton, for once, said nothing clever. He got up and stood beside her and started peeling the garlic she had been ignoring, so that the three of them worked in a row over the crate, the vapor rising off the board between them like something they had agreed to share.

The soup, when it finally went on the camp stove, was imperfect: too much thyme, one bay leaf that nobody could find afterward, and a color Benjamin chose not to comment on. But it thickened, and the smell drifted across the yard toward the fence, and Jamie closed the binder without appearing to have read it. "The tearing," she said, "it's a defense thing for the onion. The onion's trying to survive."

"Too late," Kolton said, stirring it.

Benjamin tasted it from the wooden spoon, held out a second spoonful, and watched Jamie take it. "Well?" he said.

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
knowledge_domain: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
fact: Artists commonly keep two versions of their statement: a short one of about 50 to 100 words and a longer one of about 500 to 1,000 words.
story:
The gallery on Delancey was empty except for the attendant and a woman cleaning the glass on a display case, and Eli stood in front of a painting of a flooded quarry with his phone in his hand, counting words. The wall card beside the painting held maybe sixty of them, tight paragraphs in small type, and beneath it a QR code linked to something longer. He scanned it. The full statement ran close to eight hundred words, winding through the artist's childhood in a river town, her arguments about water and memory, a paragraph about the pigments she mixed herself. So there were two of them. He had been drafting one statement for three weeks, tearing it apart, starting over, as though a single text had to do everything.

He had come here on Mr. Shapiro's advice, sort of. His art teacher had said, find a working artist's statement and read it the way you'd read a painting, which was typical of him, advice that sounded like nothing and turned out to be a map. Eli's portfolio was due in six weeks: ten pieces around one theme, plus the statement, for the scholarship application. He had eleven pieces and no theme, or rather two themes, which might be the same problem.

Theodore found him in the second room, backpack still on, breathless from the walk. "You said four o'clock."

"It's four o'clock."

"It's four-twelve." Theodore looked at the wall, at a photograph of a spillway, gray water pouring through concrete. "This the water stuff?"

"It's all water. That's the show." Eli turned his phone toward him. "Look at this. The card on the wall is short, like fifty, sixty words. But on her site there's a long one. She keeps both. The short one and a long one, the long one's like eight hundred words."

"So?"

"So the short one's for the wall, for people standing there. The long one's for applications, for people who want the whole argument." He heard himself say it and felt the small click of it, the way two drafts he'd been treating as rivals were actually two different jobs.

Theodore squinted at the phone. "Brodie's coming, by the way. He texted me from the bus."

Brodie arrived twelve minutes later with a bag of gas station snacks and immediately disagreed with the photography on principle, which was his way of entering a room. They moved through the back gallery, where the artist had hung studies, small riparian sketches in graphite, reed beds and bank lines, the kind of work that never made it onto cards. Eli kept stopping at them. His own eleven pieces came from two veins: the drawings he'd made of the drainage creek behind his grandfather's old shop, all weeds and tire water, and the cleaner, stranger paintings he'd made this year at school, abstracts he couldn't fully explain. He'd assumed the abstracts were the real ones and the creek drawings were juvenilia, something to outgrow.

"Your problem," Brodie said, through a mouthful of pretzel, "is you have the throughput of a factory and the focus of a golden retriever." He waved at the room. "She does water. Just water. Ten years of water. You could do the creek."

"The creek's not a theme. It's a place."

"So make the place the theme. What's she doing, the flooded quarry, the spillway, the river town? It's places and water. Same thing."

Eli wanted to argue and found he couldn't. The attendant drifted over, and when Theodore asked whether the artist came to the opening, she said she had, and that she'd read the long statement aloud, standing right where they were, and that people had stayed for all of it. Eli tried to picture that: reading eight hundred words to a standing crowd, no shortcut, the full length of the thinking.

They got coffee two doors down, and Eli spread his phone on the table and began drafting in his notes app, the short one first, forcing himself into the fifty to hundred word version he'd seen on the wall card. He wrote that he made drawings and paintings of one small creek, that the water in it moved through lawns and parking lots and carried whatever those places gave it, that he was trying to look at it long enough to make it strange. Theodore interposed a hand over the phone before he could delete the last line. "Keep that. The strange part. That's the good part."

The longer statement, the five hundred to a thousand words the application would actually want, he would write tonight at his desk, but he already knew its shape would be different: not a summary but an argument, the creek drawings and the abstracts laid side by side and allowed to argue with each other. He didn't know yet which one would win, or whether they had to. He had dropped one of the abstracts from the eleven, and he kept turning that over, the difference between abandoning a way of working and choosing against it for a reason. Brodie was telling a story about a substitute teacher; outside, the light was going bronze on the parked cars. Eli paid for all three coffees, pocketed his phone, and said, "Come on, I want to look at the spillway one more time before they close."

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Psychologist Robert Zajonc's 1968 experiments showed the mere-exposure effect: people tend to like things more simply because they have seen them more often.
story:
The bus route was ugly. Tyson decided this on his first morning in Marsh Creek, standing at the corner stop while the road undulated away between strip malls and dead grass, a route that seemed designed to pass every parking lot in town before it reached the school. He texted a photo of it to his friends back in Alder, captioned "view from my new life," and got back three crying-laughing emojis and nothing else. By lunch he had learned that emojis could feel like doors closing.

The school itself was fine, which was somehow worse. Fine teachers, fine hallways, a fine cafeteria where he sat with his schedule flattened on the tray like a hostage note. A boy with a sketched-upon binder sat down across from him without asking, which Tyson later understood was the local version of a welcome. "Kayson," the boy said. "You're the Alder transfer." Not a question.

At football tryouts that week, the coach ran them until the hills behind the field seemed to undulate in Tyson's vision too, and a girl named Kamila, who filmed the team for a class project, caught him dry-heaving behind the equipment shed. She handed him a water bottle and said nothing, which he appreciated more than any speech. She turned out to be taciturn the way some people are, not shy but economical, spending words like someone who had to account for each one.

The fourth week, Tyson realized he was taking the bus by choice. His mother had offered to drive him; the car was faster. But he found himself standing at the corner stop at 7:10 anyway, and when the route curved past the tire shop and the pawn place and the laundromat with the broken L, he felt something loosening in his chest that he could not explain and did not want to examine too closely, because it felt like betrayal of everyone in Alder he had sworn to miss forever.

He brought it up in the library where Kamila was logging footage. "Question," he said. "Did you ever hate something and then it just, stopped being bad? Not got good. Just stopped being bad."

"Mr. Hamdan's class," she said, not looking up. "Psych elective. There's a thing for it."

" A thing."

She pulled a textbook from her bag, thumbed to a page, and slid it across. The paragraph described experiments run by a psychologist named Robert Zajonc, published in 1968, showing the mere-exposure effect: people tend to like things more simply because they have seen them more often. Tyson read it twice.

"That's it? That's the whole trick?"

"That's the whole trick."

"So the bus route."

"The bus route," Kamila agreed.

He sat with that for a moment. It should have been insulting, he thought, the idea that his feelings could be produced by repetition like a stamping machine, that the town was not becoming likable, only familiar. But there was a second way to hold it, and he turned that over too: if exposure was doing the work anyway, he could aim it. He could choose what he saw often. The bus route, yes, but also the field at lunch, the weight room, the corner of the library where Kamila's project files lived. Familiarity could be a tool instead of something that happened to him.

He tested it that week. He stopped eating lunch alone, which was its own kind of exposure, sitting twice with Kayson and his loud friends and once with Kamila and her laptop, saying little, letting the seeing accumulate. He went to the field at lunch when it rained. He memorized the route's turns until he could predict them, the tire shop, the pawn place, the crooked laundromat sign, and the morning he caught himself smiling at the crooked L he understood that the effect did not care whether he approved of it.

On Friday his phone buzzed with a voice note from Alder, his oldest friend saying, "We're all getting pizza tonight, the usual place, you have no idea what you're missing." Tyson listened to it standing at the stop, and it hurt in the clean old way, and he let it. He typed back "have fun," which was true, and pocketed the phone.

He was not sure, yet, whether he liked Marsh Creek or merely knew it, and he suspected the experiment could not tell him the difference, which meant nobody could, possibly not even Zajonc. Kamila had said the finding held for things and even for people, which raised questions Tyson was not ready to ask out loud, about whether his friends back home were friends at all or just four years of exposure, and whether the question mattered if the result was the same.

The bus came around the curve by the tire shop, brakes gasping, doors folding open. He climbed the steps, dropped into the second seat from the back, the one that had become his without anyone assigning it, and watched the laundromat slide past with its crooked sign, waiting to find out what it would become.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: The CDC advises against washing raw chicken, because the splashing water can spread bacteria to the sink and nearby surfaces.
story:
Alyssa found the chicken in the cold case at the back of the store, wedged between trays of pork chops and a torpid stack of shrink-wrapped turkeys that looked like they had given up on something. She picked up a family pack of thighs and turned it over, reading the label as though it might tell her what to do next. Her mother had left that morning for a three-day conference, and the dinner, whole and unshared, had been handed to Alyssa: one meal, one evening, her brother and father at the table, the recipe in her mother's handwriting folded into her jacket pocket.

Theo appeared beside her with a basket of things nobody had asked him to buy, sparkling water and a bag of dried apricots. "You look like you're deciding something enormous," he said.

"I'm making dinner. Actual dinner. Rice, chicken, the green sauce from the jar in the fridge." She held the pack out so he could appreciate its weight. "My grandmother always washed the chicken first. Rinsed it in the sink, every single time, before she did anything else. So I'm going to do that."

"Elliana says you're not supposed to." Theo said it the way he said most things, lightly, as though he were offering her a mint. "She was going on about it after bio. She says washing raw chicken sprashes water around the sink and it can spread bacteria onto the counters and stuff. She said the CDC advises against it, actually."

"Sprashes?"

"Splashes. Whatever. The water splashes." He shrugged. "I don't know. I just repeat things."

Alyssa put the pack in her cart and stood there a moment. The case hummed behind her, and somewhere near the registers a cart wheel squeaked in a slow circle. She had liked the idea of the rinsing, the small ceremony of it, cold water over pale skin, the feeling of doing the thing properly that her grandmother had done properly before her. There was a kind of rectitude in it, she thought, a rightness that came from lineage rather than from evidence, and she was honest enough with herself to notice that those were not the same thing. She took out her phone, found the CDC page, and read it in the aisle while Theo pretended to compare two identical jars of paprika. The advisory was exactly what Elliana had said: washing raw chicken was not recommended, because the splashing water could spread bacteria to the sink and nearby surfaces. Nothing more, nothing less. She put the phone away.

From Theo's side of the aisle, watching her read, it looked like Alyssa was taking a quiz she had not studied for. He saw her lips move slightly over the screen, saw her glance up at nothing, and he understood that this was not about chicken for her, though he could not have said what it was about. He had known her since seventh grade and she had never once cooked anything in front of him. She had, however, once spent forty minutes explaining why her grandmother's way of folding egg whites into batter was superior to the internet's, so he kept quiet and let her finish.

They walked toward the registers together. In the produce section Alyssa picked limes and a bunch of cilantro, and the refrigerated air of the greens case had desensitized her fingers until the coins felt distant in her pocket. At the register, Ms. Tehrani from the apartment downstairs was ahead of them with a small basket, and she turned and smiled at Alyssa over the divider bar.

"Cooking tonight?" Ms. Tehrani asked, nodding at the chicken.

"First real dinner," Alyssa said. "Without my mom here."

"Brave girl," said Ms. Tehrani, and she gathered her bags and went.

At home the kitchen was quiet in the late-afternoon way, the light coming in low and yellow across the counter. Alyssa set out the cutting board, patted the chicken dry with paper towels the way the recipe said, salted it, and did not turn on the tap. Her brother came in and leaned against the fridge, eating a piece of bread he had not asked about.

"You're not washing it?" he said. "Grandma always washed it."

"I know she did," Alyssa said. She laid the thighs in the hot pan, skin side down, and the fat hissed and jumped. "The CDC says not to. The water splashes bacteria all over the sink and the counters."

Her brother chewed for a while. "So Grandma was wrong?"

"I don't know if she was wrong," Alyssa said. She pressed the chicken flat with a spatula and watched the skin begin to brown. "Maybe nobody told her either."

She stirred the rice, squeezed a lime, and stood at the stove with her hand resting on the handle of the pan. "Taste the sauce," she said, and held out the spoon.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: The Suzuki method, developed by Japanese violinist Shinichi Suzuki, teaches children to play by ear before reading music, the way they learn to speak before reading.
story:
The garage smelled of cold concrete and rosin, and Mr. Chea had bolted a music stand to the workbench because he said stands in houses always ended up broken. Seth had been coming every Thursday since September, and he could read now, could look at a page of Bach and move his fingers before the sound existed in the room. That was the part he trusted. The sound came after.

The girl arrived at six, before his slot. Her mother parked her at the bench and drove off to the store, and the girl, maybe nine, took out a half-size violin and played the piece Seth had been fighting for a month. She played it clean, the whole first movement, and when she finished she looked at the wall, not at anyone, the way kids do when they are waiting to be told it was fine.

Seth was still holding his folder of photocopies. "Can she read the chart too?" he asked Mr. Chea. He meant the sheet music clipped to the stand, the same piece, printed.

"She can't read notes at all," Mr. Chea said. He said it without apology, the way you'd say a car was a manual. The girl was already scrolling through something on a small speaker, finding her next tune.

"How does she play it, then?"

Mr. Chea nodded at the speaker. "She listens. She learned it off the recording. Same piece, same tempo, everything. She's Suzuki."

The word meant nothing to Seth, so Mr. Chea gave him only the smallest help. "Suzuki method. Shinichi Suzuki, the Japanese violinist, started it. The kids play by ear before they ever read music. Same way they learn to talk before they learn to read." Then he walked to the other bench to rehair a bow, because he was not a man who filled silence when it could fill itself.

Seth stood there with his folder. He had spent four years getting good at the part that came after the sound, the map, and this kid had gone straight for the sound and never needed the map at all. When his slot came he played from the page and got the sixteenth notes in measure thirty-four wrong twice, the same wrong notes, because his eyes kept telling his hands what to do and his hands kept almost listening.

He told Elsa about it that night on her porch, because Elsa was the one who actually wanted things. She was applying to conservatories and had opinions about everything, including him. "So learn it by ear," she said. "Record the thing, put the page away, do what she did."

"It's not that simple."

"Why not? She's nine."

He didn't have an answer that didn't sound like an excuse, so he tried it. He sat in his own garage, his father's, which smelled of motor oil instead of rosin, and played the recording through the tinny speaker of his phone thirty-one times across two nights. Without the page he felt like he was walking on a road that moved. He got the melody by the second night, then the bass line, then the middle voice, and the middle voice kept suturing itself to the wrong notes, a seam in the wrong place that he could hear but not fix, because he couldn't see where the stitches went.

On Thursday he asked Mr. Chea if he could play it without the music first, then with it. The without version fell apart in the same place as always, the moving seam. Then he set the page on the stand, found the measure, and saw the reason in four black dots: a suspension he had heard as a passing tone for two nights. The page told him what the sound was. The sound, by then, was something he already cared about, which was new, because before that week the page had been the caring and the sound had been the receipt.

"That's it," Mr. Chea said. "That whole thing you just did. Most people only ever get one of those, and they fight about which one is real."

Later, Jaeden came over with two energy drinks and sat on an overturned cooler while Seth explained, or tried to. Jaeden played nothing and believed in nothing that couldn't be timed with a stopwatch. "So which way is better?" he asked. "Sounds like the ear way is cheating."

"It's not cheating. She'll read eventually. Suzuki kids read after, not never. It's an order, not a substitution." Seth heard himself say it and heard the limits of it too, because he knew only one kid and one method and six weeks of his own ears. He had made himself a heuristic out of a single case, a rule from one data point, and he could feel the rule being useful and being flimsy at the same time.

He kept both open on the stand now, the phone propped against the sheet music, the recording running while his eyes moved. The progress was glacial after the first week, whole sessions spent on four measures, and he went back anyway. On Friday he played the movement for Elsa through the garage door, both doors open to the alley so the sound wouldn't die in the corners. He stopped once, at measure thirty-four, and started the phrase again without checking the page.

"From the top," Elsa said, and moved her chair into the doorway.

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
knowledge_domain: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
fact: Simple interest is calculated as I = P times r times t: the principal, times the annual interest rate, times the time in years.
story:
Isabella had counted the money twice on the bus, and both times it came to two hundred and forty dollars, which was enough for the phone in the window but not for the case she wanted or the month of service after the first one ended. The store smelled like carpet cleaner and new glass, and a salesman in a lanyard was already drifting toward her the way birds drift toward bread.

"Can I help you find something?"

"Just looking," she said, which was true and also a way of buying time, because she had not decided yet about her cousin's offer.

The offer was this: Dev would lend her three hundred dollars, no bank, no forms, but he wanted it back with interest, and he had named a rate that sounded small when he said it. She had told him she'd think about it, and he had laughed like thinking was a cute thing she did. Since then she had been doing the arithmetic on notebook paper during chemistry, covering the page when Simran leaned over.

Simran was already inside the store, waving from beside a display of tablets. "You came. Salma bailed, something about her mother's car. Look at this one, it has the camera you wanted."

"I know." Isabella picked up the demo phone and turned it over. The screen was bright and empty, a device showing its own home screen to no one. On the wall behind the register, a poster showed a phone broken into twelve rounded squares, each with a small price beneath it. "No interest for twelve months," the poster said, and beneath that, in type half the size, "then 29.9% on the remaining balance."

"That's a disincentive to be slow about paying," Simran said, reading over her shoulder. "My sister did one of those. She said the interest wasn't charged until it was, and then it was all at once, like a wave catching up with you."

Isabella set down the demo phone. She had written the rate Dev wanted on her hand during third period, in pen, because she kept forgetting it, and now she looked at it while Simran looked at cases. Five percent. It had sounded like nothing. Five of a hundred, nothing. But she was beginning to suspect that nothing depended entirely on how long she took to give it back.

There was a display table with a loan calculator bolted to it, a plastic thing with buttons, next to brochures about monthly plans. She typed in three hundred, then five, then one, and the machine showed her fifteen. One year, fifteen dollars. That she could picture. She typed two instead, and the number was thirty, and something in her chest loosened and then tightened again, because two years was more likely than one, the way her money went, and she remembered the formula now, the one Mr. Marino had put on the board in April while half the class slept. Principal times rate times time. She had thought it was the least germane thing anyone had ever written on a board. She had been wrong about a lot of things in April.

She tried the savings side of the same machine, the other display at the table's far end. Two hundred and forty in an account, a small rate, and the number grew instead of shrank, and she stood there holding both facts at once, the loan growing and the savings growing, the same force pulling in two directions depending on which side of it you stood. It was like standing between two mirrors.

"Did you find your phone?" Simran came back carrying a purple case she had no intention of buying.

"I found my number," Isabella said. "If I borrow three hundred at five percent and take two years to pay it back, the interest alone is thirty dollars. Three hundred times point oh five times two. That's how it works. Simple interest. Principal, rate, time."

"Is that a lot?"

"It's a month of bus fare for standing still." She looked at the phone in the window again, the exact one, silver and closed like a book. She had wanted it since March, and wanting it in March and wanting it now felt like two different weights.

"You could just wait," Simran said, and Isabella demurred, not because the idea was wrong but because waiting had its own price that no calculator displayed, all the photographs not taken, the messages arriving on her cracked old screen with its dead stripe down the middle.

The salesman drifted back, closer this time. "You folks deciding today?"

"She's deciding whether to go into debt," Simran said cheerfully.

"Everyone does," the salesman said, as if that settled something.

Isabella wrote the number on her hand, under the rate, so the two sat together: fifteen and thirty, the same loan, different patience. Then she took out her own phone, the cracked one, and typed a message to Dev, and deleted it, and typed it again. Outside, the afternoon had gone the color of a coin, and through the glass she watched a woman at the transit shelter feed the machine and miss the bus anyway.

She hit send. "How much would it be if I pay you back in six months instead of two years?"

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: On Mexico's Day of the Dead, orange marigolds called cempasúchil decorate altars and graves, because their bright color and strong scent are thought to guide the souls of the dead home.
story:
At the flower stall in the market on Twenty-Sixth Street, Violet held two bunches of marigolds and could not decide which was less ugly. The blossoms were the color of traffic cones, of melted cheddar, of everything her grandmother had refused to wear. Behind her, her cousins argued about who would carry the candles, and Amelya, who had come along only because Violet had promised her lunch afterward, kept checking her phone.

"They're all the same," Amelya said. "Orange is orange."

"It's not, though." Violet turned a stem in her hand. The petals were layered like a ruffled collar, dense and slightly wrong, like a flower designed by a committee. She had been studying the morphology of them for ten minutes, the way the heads were built, the way the stems curved, as if structure could tell her which bunch was correct. Nothing told her. The vendor watched her with the patience of a man who had sold flowers to the grieving all morning.

Her grandmother had died in August, between Violet's birthday and the start of classes, and now it was the first of November and everyone expected Violet to know what to do because she was eighteen and because she had spent the most time at the hospital. Her aunt had sent her to the market with a list and a fifty and the instruction, spoken in the doorway like a secret, that it had to be cempasúchil. Violet had written the word on her palm in pen before she remembered she could just say marigolds.

At the stall, she had asked a woman in a rebozo why it had to be those flowers, why not the white ones or the pink ones, and the woman had shrugged as if the question answered itself. "The bright color and the scent," she said, already turning back to her own shopping. "They guide the souls home." Then she was gone into the crowd, and Violet stood there holding the sentence, turning it over the way she turned the stem. Not the souls home in general. Her grandmother, specifically, from wherever she was, to the altar they were building on the dining room table out of sugar skulls and a photograph and the good tablecloth.

"Can you imagine her following a smell?" Amelya said when Violet told her. "Your grandmother hated smells. She complained about the neighbor's curry for nine years."

"That's not the point."

"Then what is the point?"

Violet set down one bunch and picked up another. The truth was that she had two ideas in her head and they did not fit together. One was her mother's, whole and untroubled: the dead come back on this night, they find the marigolds, they eat the food you leave, they know you made the altar because you love them. The other was hers, or the version of hers she'd been constructing since August, the one that said the dead do not travel, that scent is a molecule hitting a receptor, that grief is a process the brain performs on itself. And yet. And yet her grandmother's hands had been cold at the end, and Violet had kept talking to her anyway, and something in her had refused to be embarrassed about it.

She paid for the bigger bunch. The scent rose up out of the paper as she carried it, sharp and green and slightly citrus, nothing like her grandmother's lavender lotion, and Violet understood that this too was part of the arrangement, that the smell had to be strong and strange enough to travel a distance that had no measure.

Back at her aunt's house, the altar was half built. Siena, her youngest cousin, was standing on a chair pinning papel picado to the curtain rod, and their father was arguing with the caterer about whether the tamales had arrived. Violet carried the marigolds through the kitchen and the scent went ahead of her, and her mother stopped mid-sentence when she saw them, and something in her face opened and closed again.

Violet arranged the flowers along the front edge of the altar, below the photograph, scattering loose petals across the tablecloth the way the woman at the market had shown her with a quick gesture. She did not know if her grandmother could find her way here. She did not know if the petals were a path or only petals. But she had decided she would lay them down as if they were both, and that she did not need to choose, and that not choosing was not the same as not thinking.

Siena climbed down off the chair and stood beside her, chin at the level of the photograph. "Do you think she's coming tonight?"

"I think if she comes, she'll know the way," Violet said, and Siena nodded, satisfied, and reached out to straighten one orange petal with her finger.

activity: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
knowledge_domain: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
fact: Transport costs shrink the gains from comparative advantage, and if shipping a good costs more than the difference in production costs, trading it no longer pays.
story:
Maelle had claimed a table in the far corner of the food court, where the orchard of fake trees thinned out and the music from the obsolescent arcade two floors up arrived only as a rumor. Her economics textbook was open to a chapter with a diagram she had now traced with her finger four times, two curved lines crossing like birds, and Monday loomed behind it, when Ms. Traoré would make her stand at the whiteboard and explain, in her own words, why two countries both gain from trading even when one of them is better at everything. The diagram kept sliding out of her grip the way a name does in a dream. She had brought a lemon seltzer for company and the day had a thin edge of foreboding to it, the kind that comes from knowing you understand something only while you are looking at it.

Macy dropped into the opposite chair with a flyer and a purse the size of a mailbox. The flyer advertised the community fair on Saturday, and Macy's plan was a lemonade stand, first serious one, real signage, real margins. "The lemons here in the mall are four dollars a bag," she said, jabbing the grocery sign visible past the railing. "Four. Across town at the wholesale market they're two. That's half. Half, Maelle."

"Half," Maelle agreed, and tried to return to her birds.

But Macy was already leaning over the textbook, squinting at the diagram with the frank suspicion she brought to all paperwork. "Is that the thing you failed?"

"I didn't fail. I got a seventy-one."

"That's failing with manners." Macy turned the flyer over and smoothed it flat. "Just tell me the stand makes sense. Two-dollar lemons, cups at twelve cents, charge a dollar fifty. I did this on the bus."

Macy watched her friend do something she had seen maybe six times in ten years of friendship: go still, then tilt her head as though listening to a sound inside the textbook. Maelle pulled the napkin dispenser apart, took two napkins, and wrote on one, Mall lemons, $4 a bag. On the other she wrote, Market lemons, $2 a bag. Then, underneath, in smaller letters, Bus, $5 round trip. She rotated the napkins so Macy could see them side by side, the way Ms. Traoré rotated things at the board, and Macy felt her stomach drop in advance of whatever arithmetic was coming.

"You save two dollars a bag," Maelle said slowly, testing each word as if it were a plank over water. "But getting there and back costs five. So the trip costs more than what you save. It doesn't pay. And even if it did, the bus eats part of it. Transport costs shrink the gains. That's what the chapter's been trying to tell me. It's called comparative advantage, and it's only worth it if the difference is bigger than the cost of moving things."

"Is that supposed to be about countries?"

"Countries, lemonade stands, apparently the same napkin."

Finnley found them twenty minutes later, on break from the shoe store, still wearing a lanyard with a laminated nametag that said TRAINEE in a font that had given up. She listened to the napkins being presented a second time, arms crossed, then uncrossed. "I'm at that market every Saturday anyway," she said. "I could bring the lemons back with me. No bus fare, because I'm already going."

The three of them sat with that for a moment. Somewhere below, a stroller wheel squeaked past in a long arc, and the arcade's distant clatter transmuted, briefly, into something almost like applause. Macy began constructing a third napkin, this one with cups and sugar and a column headed STUFF FINNLEY DRINKS FREE, while Finnley argued the free lemonade clause down to one cup per bag.

"The whole thing rests on your Saturdays," Maelle said. "If you stop going to that market, we're back to four-dollar lemons or a five-dollar bus, and the trade stops paying. I can't tell if that means the plan is smart or fragile."

"It means," said Macy, "that I buy Finnley one lemonade and it's still cheaper than the mall, and you pass your whiteboard thing on Monday."

Saturday came blue and windy. They set up two folding tables and a hand-lettered sign whose paint ran slightly at the S, and Macy squeezed the first bag of lemons into the pitcher with a violence that suggested she was squeezing the mall grocer personally. Finnley arrived at ten with four bags in a backpack and accepted her tribute. By noon they had sold nineteen cups.

Finnley was counting the cash box when a woman from the fair committee came by, clipboard first, and asked how business was. "Excellent," Macy said. "We have a supplier."

"Local supplier?"

"Comparative advantage," Macy said, with great confidence, and stirred the pitcher.

activity: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
knowledge_domain: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
fact: Modus ponens is the valid argument form 'if P then Q; P; therefore Q', and it is valid no matter what P and Q stand for.
story:
Raphael set his fork down before he was finished, which his father noticed and pretended not to. On his phone, under the table, Alayna had sent him the problem from Mr. De Vries's class: if the wug is floop, then the ronk will zib; the wug is floop; therefore the ronk will zib. She'd added a row of question marks, and then: "Is this a joke?"

"You're not eating," his mother said.

"I'm eating." He lifted the fork again. The chicken was dry at the edges and his knife squeaked against the plate. His father had already launched into the Friday question, which was not really a question. Raphael wanted to go to the debate meetup at Noor's house, four hours, ending at eleven, and his father had opinions about eleven.

"If a boy stays out until eleven on a school night," his father said, carving air with the knife he hadn't yet used on the chicken, "then his marks suffer. It follows. It's simple."

Raphael's pulse went up, and he kept his voice flat. "That's not how it follows."

"Excuse me?"

"Your if isn't true. You just said it like it was." He heard his mother's chair creak behind him, the incipient sound of her leaving the table when the tone turned, but she stayed.

Under the table his thumb moved across the phone. He typed back to Alayna: "Check if the argument works anyway. Not whether the wug is floop. Whether the shape of it works." He set the phone face down beside his glass.

"If," his father said slowly, "his marks suffer. Which they will."

"But that's the part you haven't shown. You've shown the shape, not the stuff." Raphael could feel the warmth in his own face and hated it. "You said if marks suffer, then he's out too late, or the other way, I can't even tell which way your if goes. You flip them when it suits you."

His father put both forearms on the table. "In this house we don't need a logic course to know a school night from a Saturday."

"You sort of do, though." It came out before he could weigh it.

The tap dripped once in the silence. His mother said, "Raphael," one syllable of warning, and he watched his father's jaw work sideways, the way it did when the man was deciding whether to be a despot or merely sound like one. Raphael was sixteen; he could name the difference now, and it had stopped frightening him as much as it used to, which was its own strange loss.

"Give me one reason," his father said.

He had one, and it was the one from the wug. "Suppose you're right," Raphael said. "Suppose everything you said is true. If late, then worse marks. Fine. Then you'd still need the second part. You'd need to show he's actually out late, actually. Eleven isn't late by itself, it's late if you say school starts at seven-thirty, which it doesn't, it starts at eight-forty."

His mother almost laughed; he saw her stop it in her cheeks.

"That's slippery," his father said.

"It's the opposite. It's the least slippery thing I've said."

His phone buzzed against the wood. Alayna: "OK I did it. If the plim is dorn, then the vaz will quench. The plim is dorn. It still gets there. You can put garbage in and the shape holds." Then a second message, faster: "Mr. De Vries says it's called modus ponens."

Raphael read it twice under the table's edge, the screen's cold light on his knuckles. It was the same thing his father had done, and the same thing he himself had done, the same skeleton under both their arguments. The form carried anything you fed it: wugs or Fridays, nonsense or marks. What the form couldn't do was tell you whether the first line was true, and that was where all the fighting actually lived, at his dinner table and in every kitchen he could imagine.

"So," his father said. "Eleven. You accept my condition, or you stay home."

"Can I take the first part and still argue the second part?" Raphael asked. Not belligerent; genuinely asking, and his father blinked at the shift. "If I'm late, marks suffer. I'll grant that. Now you have to show I'd be late. Ten o'clock. Noor's mother drives. You can call her."

His mother picked up her fork and went back to the chicken as though the whole thing had been a weather report. His father looked at his son across the dry meat and the squeaking plates, and something in his face recalculated, unhappily, like a man finding the sum correct in a currency he didn't prefer.

"Ten-thirty," his father said.

"Ten-thirty," Raphael said, and picked up his fork, and ate.

Later, scraping his plate, he texted Alayna: "Does it still work if you make the second one false? Like, if the wug is floop but the ronk doesn't zib." He stood at the sink with the water running, waiting, watching the screen.

"Trying it now," she wrote back. "It does something weird. Ask Noor tomorrow."

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: On May 9, 2013, the daily average carbon dioxide level measured at Mauna Loa passed 400 parts per million for the first time in the record.
story:
Julia had been explaining the same glass jar to visitors for forty minutes, and the heat lamp was making her decision feel urgent. "So the light comes through the glass," she said, to a boy who was mainly interested in whether the jar could be opened, "and warms the air inside, but the heat has a harder time getting back out." The boy opened the jar anyway. Behind her, Murray was doing the same demo at the next table, but with sound effects, which the visitors loved and Mr. Toussaint, the education coordinator, pretended not to hear.

The demo check was at three o'clock. To earn the green lanyard that marked a real student explainer, Julia had to run the greenhouse table and then answer one question from Mr. Toussaint on the big graph, the Keeling curve blown up to poster size on the wall behind her. She knew the graph rose. She knew the line undulated as it climbed, a small yearly sawtooth riding on a long uphill slope, because Alannah had told her that word on Tuesday and Julia had liked it enough to repeat it eleven times. What she did not know was the year the line crossed 400.

She should have known. Her father, who trusted nothing he hadn't measured himself, had drilled her on the talking points in the car. Her grandmother, on the other hand, trusted everything would more or less be fine, and had drilled her on smiling. Julia suspected the truth lived somewhere between a calibration log and a smile, though she couldn't have said where, exactly, which was the problem with the truth these days.

At ten past three, Mr. Toussaint appeared with his clipboard and the gentle menace of a man who has failed many seventeen-year-olds for saying "basically." Julia did the jar first. She let him hold the thermometer. She said radiation when she meant it and warmth when she didn't. "The gases in the atmosphere let sunlight through," she said, "and absorb some of the heat radiating back up from the ground, so more of it stays near the surface than otherwise would." Then he pointed at the poster.

"And this line here," he said, tapping the place where the undulating curve crossed a horizontal line labelled 400, "what's that about?"

"That's the concentration of carbon dioxide," Julia said, "measured in parts per million, at an observatory on Mauna Loa in Hawaii. It crossed 400 for the first time in the record on May 9, 2013. The daily average."

Mr. Toussaint lowered the clipboard. "How do you know?"

"Because I got it wrong this morning," Julia said. "A man asked me and I said 2005, and he looked at me the way you look at a receipt that seems too high, and then I read the caption." Alannah, restocking brochures nearby, made a small coughing sound that meant she had witnessed the whole humiliation. "The caption says the daily average measured at Mauna Loa passed 400 parts per million for the first time in the record, on May 9, 2013. I checked it twice."

"Checking twice," said Murray, drifting over, "is not a bad habit." He looked enormously pleased with himself. "That, by the way, is litotes, understatement for effect. Julia taught me that word this week and I intend to use it until it dies."

"The graph is the graph," Alannah offered, "so honestly, checking twice is tautological." She said the word slowly, savoring it, like the last square of chocolate. "The caption says what it says."

"The caption," said Mr. Toussaint, "is not the question. The question is what she can defend." He turned back to Julia. "So the level passed 400 on May 9, 2013, at Mauna Loa. First time in the record. The daily average. And what don't you know?"

Julia looked at the sawtooth line, at the boy from earlier now trapping his sister's hand somehow inside the jar, at the little upward slope that went on regardless of anyone's morning embarrassment. "I don't know what a part per million actually looks like," she said. "I can say it, but I can't picture it. And I don't know if the man believed me when I went and found him again and told him the right year, because he just nodded and said his knee told him it was going to rain."

Mr. Toussaint wrote something on his clipboard, and then, in an act of gross unfairness, held it against his chest so nobody could read it. "Lanyard's in the office," he said. "Don't let them open the jar."

Julia went to get it, and on her way back she stopped at the poster and put her finger on the crossing point, just to feel where May 9, 2013 actually was. The boy tugged her sleeve. "Can I hold the lamp?"

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
knowledge_domain: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
fact: Gillian Flynn's 2012 novel Gone Girl alternates between two narrators, and one of them, Amy, is revealed to have written a false diary to mislead the police.
story:
Ethan had agreed to run his grandmother's book club only because she asked him in that particular voice, the one she used when her knees were worse than she admitted.
