Now he stood in her living room with nine folding chairs in a circle and a plate of lemon squares nobody had touched, watching the members arrive one by one with their copies of Gone Girl under their arms.

"Rhea's coming," his grandmother said, gripping the doorframe. "She's the one who picked it. You'll like her, she argues about everything."

He already knew Rhea from school, though she was a year ahead and moved in circles that had always seemed vaguely impermeable to him, sealed off by some social chemistry he had never bothered to decode. She arrived last, dropped into a chair, and started eating a lemon square immediately, which he found himself absurdly grateful for.

The trouble began within ten minutes. Ms. Fitzgerald, the neighbor from two doors down, held her book open to the diary chapters and said she felt cheated. "I believed her. Every page, I believed her. And then it turns out she made the whole thing up to mislead the police. How is that fair? How did the author even do that to me?"

"I finished it at two in the morning," Rhea said. "I threw the book at my wall."

Ethan had read the novel twice, once for himself and once because his English teacher had set a paper on point of view, and it was the one assignment this year he hadn't wanted to finish. He found, standing there with the plate of lemon squares, that he had two completely different things in his head and no idea yet whether they could be made to sit together. One was his teacher's line, that an unreliable narrator is a technical problem, that you track the slippage between what the narrator claims and what the evidence on the page allows. The other was his own memory of reading the diary chapters on the bus, his throat tightening, the genuine sympathy he had felt for a woman who did not exist.

"I don't think it's a trick exactly," he said slowly. "It's more like the author split the book in half. The chapters alternate between two narrators, and one of them is Amy, and the diary you were trusting is hers."

"But it's fake," Ms. Fitzgerald said.

"It's fake inside the story. That's the part I keep turning over. The diary isn't lying to you, the character wrote it to lie to the police."

His grandmother, sunk deep in her armchair with her bad leg propped on a cushion, caught his eye and gave him a small nod, the kind she gave across dinner tables when he was seven and not sure whether to try the escalator alone.

Rhea leaned forward. "So when did you stop believing her?"

"That's the embarrassing part. Not until the book told me to." He turned his own copy over in his hands. "For the paper I had to go back and find the moments where the narration didn't add up, and they're there, but I missed all of them the first time. I wanted to believe her. The diary chapters are written to make you want to."

"And that's bad," Ms. Fitzgerald said.

"I don't know that it's bad." He heard the hesitation in his own voice and let it stand. "My teacher would say it's a device. Track the evidence, notice the gaps. But that's like saying you should read with armor on so nobody can get to you. If you read like that you're safe and you're also alone the whole time." He glanced at Rhea, who was watching him without the faint boredom he'd feared. "Maybe the honest position is that you have to get tricked first. You can't see the structure until after you've felt the pull of it."

The room went quiet in the way rooms do when someone has said a true thing awkwardly.

"Then we were all doing it right," Rhea said. "Getting tricked, I mean." She looked around the circle. "Raise your hand if you believed the diary." Eight hands went up, including his grandmother's, raised with a certain defiance. Ms. Fitzgerald raised hers last, and Rhea said, "There. We're not fools, we're the intended readers. The book needed us exactly as gullible as we were."

Ethan wrote that down on the folded sheet of notes he'd brought, because it seemed like something he'd want later. It also seemed, in some way he couldn't yet articulate, to be in tension with what he'd written for the paper, and he liked the feeling of holding both of them, not forcing them to agree.

Afterward, while the members filed out with their plates wrapped in foil, his grandmother asked him to carry the folding chairs to the garage. Rhea stayed to stack them with him, matching his pace, sliding each chair into the rack with a small clang. In the dim garage she said, "I stigmatized you, you know. At school. I thought you were just the quiet kid who was good at English and looked down on everyone for it."

"I probably looked down on everyone for it."

She laughed and pushed the last chair home. "Next month's my pick too. Something you'll definitely hate." She pulled out her phone and showed him the cover before he could brace himself. "An acolyte narrator. Whole book narrated by a guy who worships the main character and never notices what she's actually doing. My cousin says you can't trust a word of it." She held the screen there, waiting, her thumb over the button. "So. Are you in?"

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
knowledge_domain: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
fact: Claude Monet painted more than thirty views of the facade of Rouen Cathedral in 1892 and 1893, showing it under different light at different times of day and year.
story:
Julia spread the ten sketches across the kitchen table and pushed the fruit bowl to the far end to make room. Every drawing was of the maple in the backyard: dawn, dusk, one in fog, one after rain, one in February when the branches were bare and looked like writing she could not read.

Her mother set down a mug of tea and looked over her shoulder. "They're all the same tree."

"That's the point," Julia said. "Maybe."

Ms. Fischer had assigned the portfolio on Monday: ten artworks, one theme, an artist's statement of a page. "A theme is not a subject," she had said, tapping the handout. "A subject is what you drew. A theme is what you are asking." Julia had written three drafts of her statement and deleted each one, because she could not answer what she was asking, or whether painting the same tree at different hours counted as asking anything at all.

Lydiane arrived at four with her own portfolio under her arm, half-finished, and sat down across from Julia without being asked. Lydiane's theme was memory: her grandmother's hands, a bus stop from childhood, a coat on a hook. She wanted to be certain of it. "I need you to tell me it's cohesive," she said, laying the pieces out in a row. "Thomas said it's just nostalgia. He said I should pick something bigger, like identity or climate, something with scope."

"Thomas's portfolio is about entropy," Julia said. "He's doing photographs of rust."

"That has scope. Rust is universal."

The two of them looked at Julia's row of trees. Lydiane picked up the February one and held it at arm's length. "This is the best one. But are you allowed to just do one thing ten times?"

Julia took her phone and typed the question into the search bar the way she typed everything, half expecting nothing. What she found she read twice. Claude Monet had painted more than thirty views of the facade of Rouen Cathedral in 1892 and 1893, showing it under different light at different times of day and year. More than thirty. She turned the phone around on the table so Lydiane could see the images, the same stone frontage going pink, then gold, then a bruised grey, as though the building were the one moving.

"There," Lydiane said. "So it's allowed."

"It's not about allowed." Julia pulled the phone back and scrolled. "He wasn't repeating it. The light was the subject and the cathedral was just the thing the light landed on." She looked at her own sketches again, the dawn one and the dusk one side by side, and understood that what she had been recording was not the tree at all. The tree was her excuse for the sky behind it. She said this out loud, and Lydiane frowned, and Julia heard how it sounded, like a line from a statement she hadn't written yet.

That evening Thomas came over with rust on his mind and a complaint about Ms. Fischer. "She told me entropy is a theme but rust is a subject," he said, taking a chair and turning it backwards before sitting. "So I'm doing it on decay now. Decay is the theme." He ate three of the biscuits meant for all of them and argued that Julia's ten trees were a cop-out, that a real portfolio showed range. "You could draw anything," he said. "Why the same tree ten times?"

"Monet painted more than thirty views of the facade of Rouen Cathedral," Julia said, "in 1892 and 1893, under different light at different times of day and year."

Thomas went quiet for a second, then said, "That's different, that's Monet."

"Okay," Julia said, and poured more tea.

After he left she sat alone at the table with the lamps off and the porch light throwing a long shadow of the maple across the sketches, so that the shadow of the tree lay over the drawings of the tree. She moved one paper and the shadow undulated across the rest, slower than wind would have moved it. Her ennui from the afternoon, which had felt permanent, thinned into something more like patience. She took out a fresh sheet and began the eleventh drawing, the same maple, but this time with the porch light in it, the anachronistic yellow glow of a subdivision at night falling on branches that had been standing there since before the street had a name.

Lydiane texted at eleven: decided to keep memory, grandmother's hands and all. Thomas can have decay. Julia typed back a thumbs up, then deleted it and wrote, it's cohesive, which was true, and set the phone face down.

She worked on the statement last, one paragraph, and left the second paragraph blank because she was not yet sure whether the theme was light or time or the fact of watching one thing long enough that it stopped being one thing. She would find out when the series was done, or she would not, and either way the drawings would be on the table in the morning, the shadow of the tree moving over them as the sun came up on the far side of the house.

activity: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
knowledge_domain: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
fact: In the United States, most negative information on a credit report, such as late payments, can be reported for seven years, and bankruptcies for up to ten.
story:
The admissions table for the business school had a bowl of mints shaped like little coins, which Jordyn took as either a joke or a warning. She was eighteen and had driven two hours with her mother to this open house because she had been accepted to three places and could only afford to visit one, and this was the one with the best financial aid letter. The letter sat folded in her back pocket like a verdict she hadn't read closely enough.

Hussein was already there, leaning against a pillar outside the student activities fair, scrolling his phone with the particular slouch of someone who had driven up with a different group and was pretending he hadn't seen anyone. He and Jordyn had survived AP Economics together, which mostly meant surviving each other's study habits. "Don't tell me you're doing the finance track," he said when she walked over.

"Undeclared. They make you declare a loan instead."

He laughed, then winced and held up his phone. "Speaking of loans. My card declined on gas this morning and it turns out I missed a payment last month. Forty dollars. They already sent me some letter with the words 'credit bureau' in it, like I'm being summoned."

"Did you pay it?"

"I'll pay it eventually. It's forty dollars. It's not like they send you to jail."

Skyla materialized beside them wearing a lanyard she'd gotten from a club she had no intention of joining, the way you collect shells at a beach you'll never return to. "What's forty dollars?"

"Nothing," Hussein said. "That's the point."

At the financial literacy booth, a student volunteer in a maroon polo was stacking pamphlets, and Jordyn drifted toward her the way you drift toward a free sample. The booth had a poster with a cartoon dollar bill wearing a graduation cap. Ms. Ba, whose name was printed on the volunteer badge, turned out to be a second-year who worked the booth on Saturdays and had the flat, unimpressed tone of someone who had explained the same thing forty times before lunch.

"Do you have a question," Ms. Ba said, "or are you taking mints again."

"She has a question," Hussein said, delighted to volunteer someone else. "I missed a credit card payment and I want to know if I should care."

Ms. Ba looked at him over the pamphlets. "In the United States, most negative information on a credit report, like late payments, can be reported for seven years. Bankruptcies, up to ten."

"Seven years," Hussein repeated, as though the number had personally insulted him. "I'll be, like, twenty-five."

"You'll be renting apartments at twenty-five," Jordyn said. "Applying for leases. Car loans, if you get a job that needs a car." She hadn't planned to say any of it; it came out in the flat cadence of the pamphlets themselves.

"That's so dramatic. One late payment."

"One that gets reported," Ms. Ba said, and straightened the stack.

Jordyn took a pamphlet even though she didn't want it, mostly to have something in her hands. On the walk to the residence hall tour she found herself sorting things, the way she did when a problem wouldn't sit still: the categories weren't debt versus no debt, or careful versus careless. There was a taxonomy underneath the obvious one, something like decisions whose consequences you can feel immediately, and decisions whose consequences arrive on a delay so long you stop believing in them. Forty dollars at the pump was one kind of event. A number in a database, patiently waiting seven years, was a different species entirely, and Hussein kept treating them as the same animal.

"The thing is," Hussein said, catching up to her outside the tour, "my cousin says everybody's credit is bad at our age. It's basically a rite of passage."

"Your cousin also says you can outrun a bear."

"Mostly you just have to outrun the slowest person."

She let that stand, because it was a fair point about bears and no kind of point at all about credit bureaus. Still, she could feel her own position assembling itself from two directions at once: her mother's voice, which treated every dollar as something that could turn on you when you weren't looking, and Hussein's, which treated the whole system as a game with a rigged scoreboard and therefore not worth respecting. Jordyn didn't fully believe either one. The seven years felt real to her, dense, a weight she could sense through the folded paper of the pamphlet in her pocket. But she also suspected that a life organized entirely around numbers you couldn't see would be a cramped one, a life spent flinching at a future that might be evanescent anyway, dissolving the moment you got close enough to touch it.

"I'm going to pay it," Hussein said suddenly. "Today. There's an app."

"There's an app for everything."

"You don't have to sound like my mother."

"I don't. Your mother would say seven years is nothing. She'd mean it as a threat."

He was already tapping at his phone, thumbs moving with the urgency he'd never shown an English essay. Skyla appeared with a snow cone from somewhere, blue, already melting down her wrist, and asked what she'd missed, and Jordyn opened her mouth to say something tidy about it.

"The tour's leaving," said the guide, and Jordyn turned and followed the group through the doors, the pamphlet still folded in her pocket, unread.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: ISO 216 paper sizes such as A4 have sides in the ratio of 1 to the square root of 2, so cutting a sheet in half gives two sheets of the same shape.
story:
The art shed at Camp Wren smelled of cedar shavings and glue, and Cole had claimed the far table by arriving ten minutes early every morning. His project was a poster for the end-of-summer fair: a map of the camp with trails, the lake, the dining hall, and small drawn figures where events would happen. He wanted it big enough to read from the road. He had drawn it at A4 size on a single sheet, tight and careful, because that was the paper the shed supplied.

Roxanne leaned over his shoulder on Wednesday. "That's good, but nobody's going to see a stick figure drowning in the lake at that size. You need it huge."

"The library in town has a self-serve printer," Mackenzie said. She was folding paper cranes three tables over, badly, and had been listening. "My brother printed his band flyers there. You scan your drawing and blow it up."

Roxanne, who considered herself an epicure of all things visual, food, fonts, sunsets, was skeptical of any enlargement. "It never works. It gets blurry, or the edges get cut off, and it looks like the machine ate it." She held up a flyer from her old school, its border sliced through mid-letter, as evidence.

On Thursday their counselor, Mr. Murphy, drove Cole and Mackenzie into town in the camp van. The library printer offered two paper sizes: A4 and A3, which was the next size up. Cole scanned his poster, sent it to the machine, and chose A3, since bigger was the whole point.

The machine blinked at him. A notice on the screen said the design's proportions did not match the chosen paper, and offered options: fit to page, fill page, or crop. Fit to page left a white band along the top. Fill page cut off the dining hall and half the lake. Crop was worse.

"That's Roxanne's machine-eating thing," Mackenzie said, watching the preview screen. "Maybe she was right and you just redraw it big."

Cole stood there while the printer hummed, waiting for him. He measured his drawing with a ruler he'd brought. Eight and a quarter inches by eleven and three quarters. He picked up a fresh A4 sheet from the free stack beside the machine and measured it. Then he held his drawing against the A3 paper in the tray, corner to corner, and saw that the A3 sheet was exactly the same shape as the A4, just larger. Not almost. Exactly.

He opened the settings on the printer and looked up the sizes. A4 and A3 were both part of ISO 216, a standard he'd never heard of, and the sides were in a ratio of one to the square root of two. He said it out loud to make it real. "One to root two." That was why the shapes matched. Mackenzie, reading over his arm, pointed at a line on the help screen: it also meant that if you cut a sheet in half, you got two sheets of the same shape as the one you started with.

"So the big one is the small one doubled," Mackenzie said. "Not stretched. Doubled."

He set the scale to exactly two hundred percent, chose A3, and pressed print. The machine fed the sheet through once and delivered the poster at the far side, warm and clean. The map covered the whole page edge to edge. No white band, no missing dining hall. He laid it on the table and put his original beside it, and every line fell where it should, only twice as large. Mackenzie put her hand flat on the lake. "Your drowning guy is visible from space now."

He paid his sixty cents at the desk, and they walked out to where Mr. Murphy was reading the local paper in the van.

That night Roxanne inspected the poster under the shed's fluorescent light. "Okay," she said. "I was wrong about blurring. But I still think it's specious to call it bigger art. It's the same drawing, just farther away from your face." Cole started to argue, then stopped, because she wasn't entirely wrong. The poster was his same small decisions, the same hesitant ink line on the dock, magnified. Nothing new had been added.

He sat with that while the other campers drifted in for evening craft time. On the table lay the spare A3 sheet he'd bought, and beside it a pair of scissors. He picked up the scissors, folded the big sheet once, and cut it in half. Two A4 sheets, each with the same proportions as the one he'd divided. He cut one of those in half and got two smaller ones, still the same shape. He kept cutting, down to pieces the size of a postcard, then a business card, a stack of identical rectangles shrinking toward the lamp.

Roxanne watched him do it without saying anything. When he reached pieces too small to fold accurately, he stopped and lined them all up, largest to smallest, along the edge of the table.

"Those would be good as fair invitations," she said. "The little ones. People could put them in a pocket."

He turned the smallest piece over in his fingers. It was blank on both sides, and exactly the same shape as everything above it in the line. "Print the little map on all of them," he said. "Same drawing, every size. One for every table at the fair."

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Acrylic paint is water-based while wet, but it dries quickly and becomes water-resistant once dry.
story:
Robert had signed up for the Tuesday open studio because his mother said he needed somewhere to put his hands, and because Mr. Horváth had mentioned, offhand and twice, that community college transcripts looked better with something on them. He was gluing slats of balsa wood into a frame for a lampshade, a project he'd been planning since March, when he found a design in a library book about Danish interiors and decided, with the certainty available only to someone who had never built anything, that it would be simple.

It was not simple. The slats warped as the glue set, and the lampshade was becoming, in his hands, a shape that resembled a crushed paper cup. Across the table, River was painting a canvas in colors that shouldn't have worked together and somehow did, violent orange under a wash of gray green, and Marie-Soleil was sketching the same ceramic teapot for the third time because, she said, the first two had lied.

"Lied how," Robert asked.

"The spout looked cooperative. It wasn't."

He liked them both in different ways. River worked like weather, sudden and total, while Marie-Soleil worked like a lawyer, cross-examining her own lines. Robert himself wanted a system. He had measured everything twice, cut once, drawn diagrams in a notebook with a ruler his father had given him for no occasion at all. The problem was that the diagrams assumed the world would hold still, and balsa wood, it turned out, had opinions.

Mr. Horváth circulated with his coffee, pausing at each table like a man checking on soup. At River's canvas he said nothing, only nodded, which River accepted as a standing ovation. At Robert's frame he crouched, looked along the slats, and said, "You're fighting the material."

"I'm directing it."

"Mm." He moved on. Robert hated the mm. It was worse than criticism because you had to supply the criticism yourself.

He decided the lampshade needed a painted panel, something translucent, and went to the shelf where the studio kept its communal paints. He chose a pale blue, watered it down in a jar the way he'd seen River do, and brushed a test strip onto a scrap of canvas. During the break, when everyone went outside to eat their sandwiches in the October sun, he left his brush resting across the jar rim, bristles dipped in the blue, and forgot about it for forty minutes while River explained, with diagrams drawn in mustard on a napkin, why a person who refused to share their fries was, quote, "a pure egoist, the last of a dying breed."

When Robert came back, the brush had become an artifact. The bristles had set into a single stiff blue ridge, like a tiny glacier. He tried rinsing it under the tap, working it with his fingers, and nothing moved. The blue wouldn't come out and the hairs wouldn't separate.

"Dead," Marie-Soleil said, watching him scrub. "That one's gone."

"It's paint. Paint washes out with water. It's practically water."

"Not this kind." She took the jar, tilted it so he could read the label. "Acrylic. It's water-based while it's wet, so you can thin it, but it dries fast, and once it's dry it's water-resistant. You have about ten minutes, maybe, and then it's permanent."

Robert held the ruined brush under the light. There was something almost captivating about the failure, the way the bristles had frozen mid-gesture, and he felt a visceral twist of annoyance at himself, not at the paint. The paint had done exactly what the paint does. He was the one who had assumed the rules of one material applied to another.

He soaked the brush in a cup anyway, out of a stubbornness he recognized, and while it sat there not softening, he found a fresh brush, thinned the blue properly, and painted his panel in one uninterrupted pass, rinsing immediately, keeping the bristles submerged between coats in a jar of water like a surgeon keeping instruments ready. River watched this procedure with open delight. "Look at him. Fifty seconds ago he murdered a brush and now he's running a hospital."

The panel dried fast, faster than he expected, which meant he had to work in sections instead of blending, and the seams showed. He stood back and looked at them. He thought about River's canvas, which was all seams and impulses, and about Marie-Soleil's teapot, drawn three times in order to be honest, and about his diagrams, which were beautiful and useless. Maybe the lampshade was allowed to be a record of decisions rather than a proof of a plan. He didn't know if that was wisdom or just lowering the bar, and he was honest enough with himself to leave the question open.

He glued the panel into the frame, warped slats and all. It sat crooked, catching the afternoon light through pale blue, throwing a wobbly rectangle on the table that looked, Marie-Soleil said, like a lake seen from a plane. River put a fry on top of it as a dedication. Robert tilted the frame until the light lay along the seams, and said, "Same time Tuesday."

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In the CDC's 2021 Youth Risk Behavior Survey, about 1 in 12 US high school students who had dated reported experiencing physical dating violence.
story:
Isla had tried on three shirts before deciding that the gray one, the one she almost never wore, was the one, and she could not have said why. The date was small, almost embarrassingly small: Anis was coming to her house at seven, where her mother would be home the whole time, and they were going to make pizza from a kit and watch a movie on the couch. It was still a first date. It still counted. She stood at the mirror and pulled her hair back, then let it down again, and through the window the October light lay flat and pale across the yard like something out of the documentary her geography teacher had shown them about the steppe, that enormous grassland where the horizon never once broke.

Maelys arrived at six with a bag of sour candies and the manner of someone who had rehearsed a speech in the car. She sat on Isla's bed, sorted the candies by color without being asked, and said nothing for a while. "You look nice," she said finally. "Very gray. Very cool." Then she snapped a candy in half and looked at the halves instead of at Isla.

"Say it," Isla said.

"Friday. In the hallway by the gym." Maelys turned one of the candy halves over in her fingers. "When you told him you had to leave early. He grabbed your arm. Like that." She closed her hand around her own wrist to show it, and the demonstration was worse than the memory had been, because it made the thing separate from Isla, an object she could look at from across the room.

"He was excited," Isla said. "We were laughing about something. It wasn't a thing."

"Okay." Maelys did not say okay like she believed it. She said it like she was setting it down carefully, the way you set down a full glass. Then she said, "We did this unit in health last semester. Physical dating violence. It's more common than people think. In the CDC's 2021 Youth Risk Behavior Survey, about 1 in 12 US high school students who had dated reported experiencing it." She recited it flatly, the way she recited debate statistics, and then her voice went ordinary again. "That's not a reason to cancel. I know that's not what a number means. It's just a thing I know now that I can't unknow."

Isla sat down at her desk chair and looked at the poster above it, the one with the horses running across the steppe, which she had bought at a museum two years ago and never taken down. She understood what Maelys was doing, and it irritated her, and it also did something she could not quite resent: it took the blurry feeling from Friday, the one she had folded up small and put away, and gave it edges. The statistic reified nothing on its own, she thought; numbers did not reach into hallways. But a number could give you permission to look at a thing straight instead of sideways. Maybe the grab was nothing. Maybe it was the first inch of something. Both of those could be true from where she was sitting, and the honest position, she decided, was not to pretend she knew which one.

"I'm not canceling," Isla said. "He's a person, not a data point. But I'm going to say something tonight if it happens again. Not a big speech. Just, don't do that."

"Okay," Maelys said again, and this time it sounded like she believed it.

Downstairs, the doorbell rang at 6:58, and Maelys was the one who reached it first, because Isla was still deciding between leaving her hair down and putting it up, a decision that felt seismic to her and looked like nothing at all. From the hallway, Maelys watched Anis step in out of the cold, shaking rain off his jacket, holding a paper bag that turned out to contain the exact sour candies she had brought, which made everyone laugh and broke something open in the room.

Maelys stayed for the first twenty minutes, mostly for the pizza assembly, and she watched the small things: how Anis rolled the dough badly and laughed at his own hands, how he moved the pepperoni around into a smiley face, how he sat on the far end of the couch without asking where to sit. When she left, Isla walked her to the door, and they stood for a second under the porch light with the rain ticking in the hedge.

"You're okay?" Maelys said, not as a question exactly, more as a hand held out.

"I'm okay," Isla said. "And if I'm not, I'll tell you on Tuesday."

"That's all I wanted," Maelys said, and went down the steps into the rain, pulling her hood up, and Isla watched until she turned the corner before she went back inside, where Anis was pausing the movie to wait for her, one hand curled loosely around the remote, the other resting open on the empty cushion beside him.

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: Under the 2017 American guideline, stage 1 hypertension means a systolic reading of 130 to 139 or a diastolic reading of 80 to 89.
story:
The cuff hissed twice before Raphael got the hang of it, and by the third try his grandfather's arm bore the pink crease of a beginner's enthusiasm. It was the second week of August, the week before Raphael left for college, and he had volunteered for this the way he volunteered for anything at the house on Delancey Street: not out of tenderness exactly, but out of a suspicion that if he did not do it, no one would.

The monitor had arrived in the spring, a gift from an aunt who meant well and then vanished back into her own life. His grandfather logged the readings in a school notebook, three columns in his engineer's hand, and it was this notebook Raphael asked to see while the kettle worked itself up to a whistle.

"You doing homework on me now?" his grandfather said, but he slid it across the table without waiting for an answer.

Raphael had spent the summer working as a counselor at a day camp, and the one thing he had retained from the orientation was a demonstration they made every counselor perform: take a reading, say it back in plain words, explain what a person could actually do about it. He had done it forty times for teenagers who giggled at the cuff. He had never once done it for someone whose numbers he cared about.

The notebook opened at July. He ran his thumb down the systolic column and felt the mild vertigo of real data, as opposed to the practice numbers he'd been handed in a gymnasium. One thirty-four. One twenty-eight. One thirty-six again, then one forty, then one twenty-nine. The diastolic column sat mostly in the low eighties. He had read the guideline the night before orientation, more thoroughly than he had read anything since, and now he recited it under his breath like a defense attorney checking precedent. Stage one hypertension meant a systolic reading of 130 to 139, or a diastolic reading of 80 to 89. Below that, you were fine, or fine enough. Above it, you were something else.

His grandfather was watching him from across the table, and Raphael realized he had gone quiet too long, that his face was doing arithmetic the old man could read.

"Well?" his grandfather said. "Say it. You've got that look your mother gets before she tells me something's wrong with the car."

"Most of these are in the 130s," Raphael said. "Top number. And the bottom ones are mostly low 80s."

"And?"

He turned the notebook toward the window so the light caught the ink. He wanted, badly, to be able to say this was nothing. He had spent the drive over composing a speech about diet and walking that now seemed almost gratuitous, a performance of concern that would let him feel useful without having to ask anything hard. "Stage one hypertension means systolic 130 to 139 or diastolic 80 to 89," he said. "That's the 2017 guideline. Under it, most of your page counts."

The kettle screamed. Neither of them moved.

What Raphael could not see, and did not think to look for, was the second notebook, the one with the marbled cover, shelved between the cookbooks where a grandson would never browse. His grandfather knew it was there. He had been keeping two logs since June: the school notebook for the numbers he was willing to show, and the marbled one for the rest.

The old man stood, poured the water over tea bags, and carried both mugs back with the unhurried deliberateness he used to buy time. He had watched his own father get a diagnosis at sixty-eight and get disenfranchised by it, so gradually it took years to notice: first the driving, then the stairs, then whole categories of food policed by a wife who loved him and a doctor who didn't know his middle name. He had decided, somewhere in June, that he would rather be a man with a slightly forgettable notebook than a man with a file.

"So I should eat less salt," he said. "Walk more. I know the speech."

"It's not a speech," Raphael said, and then, because he was eighteen and honest by reflex, "okay, it's partly a speech. But it's true. Salt, walking, the readings change. They showed us the data at camp. It's not dramatic, but it moves."

"How much does it need to move?"

"Ten points down and you're out of that range on the top number. But that's not really the point." Raphael put his hand flat on the notebook. "The point is you haven't been to the doctor since Easter, and you know that, and I know that, and I'm leaving Saturday."

There it was, then. The chronology mattered more than either of them had admitted: the readings had been climbing since spring, and the last professional set of eyes on the man across the table had belonged to someone who had seen him in March, before any of this. Raphael understood suddenly that his grandfather had not been careless. He had been choosing, month by month, entry by entry, and the choice had a logic that Raphael could respect and still refuse to leave undisturbed.

His grandfather looked at his mug for a long moment. Then he got up, went to the shelf between the cookbooks, and took down the marbled notebook. He set it beside the first one without a word, and Raphael opened it and saw the numbers he had been spared: one forty-two, one thirty-eight, one forty-four.

"Saturday," his grandfather said. "Before you go."

Raphael took out his phone and started looking for available appointments.

"You can drive me Tuesday," the old man said. "And you can tell that doctor the salt speech yourself. I want to watch you do it."

activity: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
knowledge_domain: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
fact: The three primary chords of a major key are built on its first, fourth and fifth notes, so in C major they are C, F and G.
story:
The garage smelled of motor oil and old carpet, and Mr. Ramírez's keyboard sat on a workbench between a toolbox and a box of fencing wire. Jade had claimed it every Tuesday since September, but tonight was different: the melody had to be finished and written out, all sixteen bars with chord changes above the staff, by Friday's composition showcase. She had three days and eight empty measures.

Lane arrived with his guitar before she had written a note, ducking under the half-open door with his amp cord wrapped around his fist. He could only really play three chords, which he changed between with the concentration of someone defusing something, and he had a way of making even that sound like a decision rather than a limitation. He plugged in, struck a chord, and Jade looked up from her blank staff paper.

"Okay," she said. "Play what you have."

He played C, then F, then back to C, then G. The progression was simple, but something about the way the G pushed back toward the C made her sit up. "Do that again." He did. She wrote the letters above the first four bars of her staff, one letter per measure, and hummed a note against each one until she found sounds that belonged and a few that didn't, which interested her more.

"You're building your whole melody on my three chords," Lane said, half pleased and half embarrassed. "That's like arbitrage. You found something cheap and you're trading up."

"It's not cheap if it works," she said, but she was already flipping through the theory book Mr. Ramírez had left on the bench, the one with coffee rings on the circle-of-fifths page. She found a diagram and stopped. The three chords Lane knew, the ones that sounded like they wanted to go home, weren't a random accident of his limited guitar skills. The primary chords of a major key were built on its first, fourth, and fifth notes. She counted it out on the keys. First, fourth, fifth. In C major, that was C, F, and G. Lane had taught himself the spine of the whole key without knowing it had a name.

She played the pattern herself, C and F and G, listening for where each one pulled. Then she tried the trick her mother's querulous neighbor had complained about through the fence last summer, the vi-IV-V-I from some song he hated, and it didn't fit what Lane had shown her, and she put it aside. Not everything had to be borrowed. She hummed a small stepwise figure over the C, let it rise when the chord changed to F, and drop when it came to G, and for four bars the melody seemed to walk on its own.

Bars nine through twelve were where it fell apart. She wanted a bridge, something that lifted, but every note she tried against the F sounded like a weaker copy of the opening. Lane leaned over the keyboard and played the chords louder, as if volume could substitute for an idea, and she laughed and shoved his elbow off the bench. Then she tried the opposite of what she'd been doing: instead of writing a melody and hanging chords under it, she wrote the chords first, all the way to bar sixteen, and let the melody find its own reasons. The G chord in bar fourteen gave her a note she never would have chosen on purpose. She circled it.

"That's the one," Lane said.

"Maybe." She wrote it in standard notation, the stem directions wrong at first, then corrected, the beamed eighth notes cramped until she eased them apart. She couldn't tell yet whether the melody was actually good or whether she had spent so long inside it that she'd started to internalize its logic, the way you stop noticing your own handwriting. That was the part she couldn't test alone. Tomorrow she'd play it for Mr. Ramírez, who would tell her the truth, which was what she wanted and also dreaded.

She copied the last bar, wrote the chord letters in a neat column above the staff, and set her pencil down. Lane played the progression once more, soft, and Jade sang the melody over it, all sixteen bars, slower than it would be on Friday, and stopped on the final C.

"Again," she said. "From the top."

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: In gleaning programs, food bank volunteers harvest crops that remain in farm fields after the main harvest, food that would otherwise go to waste.
story:
The soup kitchen smelled of onions and bleach, and Emma stood in the doorway for a moment before anyone noticed her. She had signed up because the college application was done and her mother kept saying she should do something that wasn't for the application, which struck Emma as a paradox she hadn't solved yet: the moment a good act stopped counting, did it count more, or had she only changed who was keeping score?

"You're new," said a woman behind the serving counter, reading her hesitation as lostness rather than philosophy. "Aprons are on the hook. You're with the Saturday group."

The Saturday group turned out to be three people her own age: Nika, who had volunteered here for two years and moved through the kitchen like she owned the dish rack, and Zachery, who was on his phone until Ms. Novák, the coordinator, took the sign-up sheet out of his hands and pointed him toward the industrial cans of crushed tomatoes. Ms. Novák explained the morning in fragments while they worked. Prep until ten, then the van, then the farm.

"The farm?" Emma asked. She had pictured ladling soup, not leaving the building. "I thought we'd be here."

"Some Saturdays we go out to the fields," Nika said, without looking up from the cutting board. "You'll see."

The van rattled west past the edge of town, and Ms. Novák drove with two fingers on the wheel, narrating the landmarks the way people do when they've driven a route so many times it has become a kind of private text. Zachery asked what they would actually be doing out there. Emma watched the fields slide past, the stubble and the fence lines, a cluster of dark stones in a cleared lane that she guessed were igneous, carried down from somewhere northern by ice or water, though she couldn't have said which and liked not knowing.

At the farm, a squat man in a seed cap met them at the gate and led them to a field of squash. The main harvest had gone out two weeks earlier, he said. The trucks had taken what the buyers wanted, the uniform ones, and what was left had been lying there since. Emma had expected a few stragglers. Instead there were hundreds: crooked butternuts, acorn squash with a scab of frost damage on one side, a pumpkin split along a seam like a badly sewn seam. All of it had been invisible from the road.

"So we're just picking up the rejects," Zachery said, crouching beside a lopsided butternut.

"It's called gleaning," Nika said. "We harvest what's left in the field after the main harvest, food that would otherwise go to waste." She said it lightly, the way you'd say the name of a bus route, and moved down the row.

They worked in a line, filling crates, and Emma found a rhythm in it, the twist and lift, the small judgment of which squash was worth taking. She began to wonder about the judgment itself. The frost-scabbed ones were fine inside, Ms. Novák said when she asked, you just cut that part away. Emma turned one over in her hands and thought about how the buyers had decided it was worthless and how the decision had almost become true, how close food comes to garbage simply because someone with a checklist says so. It reminded her of the soup kitchen that morning, where the same word, reject, seemed to hover over everything, and where nobody said it because saying it would stigmatize the people eating, and not saying it let a different kind of silence do the work instead.

By noon they had filled the van's back bench with crates, and the farmer waved them off without getting out of his truck. In the passenger seat, Ms. Novák tallied the poundage on a clipboard. Emma asked her why the farmer didn't just do this himself, why it needed volunteers, and Ms. Novák shrugged and said labor costs money and squash doesn't, not anymore, not this late. It was an answer that opened a door onto something Emma stood looking into for a while. The waste wasn't carelessness exactly; it was arithmetic. And here she was, and here they all were, donating hours to fix an arithmetic problem that had been created by the same economy that made squash cheap enough to abandon. She felt something that was not quite guilt and not quite pride, a complicity she couldn't locate precisely, since she had neither set the prices nor planted the field, and yet had eaten cheap squash her whole life without once asking what made it cheap.

Back at the kitchen, they washed the squash in the deep sink and Ms. Novák cubed it for tomorrow's soup, and the pile of salvage grew on the steel counter until it looked less like salvage and more like dinner. Zachery photographed it. Nika told him nobody wanted to see his squash pictures and then leaned in to check the framing. Emma took the peel bucket out to the compost and stood for a minute in the alley, where the light was going thin and gray.

She hadn't resolved anything, she decided, walking back in. The volunteering was good and the volunteering was also a patch on a system nobody in the van had designed, and both of those could be true at once, the way the squash was both rejected and perfectly good, depending on who was holding it. She would come back next Saturday. She would also, maybe, take an economics elective in the fall, though she wasn't sure yet whether she wanted to understand the system or just to be able to argue with it. Inside, Ms. Novák was ladling out the last of the onion soup, and she looked up when Emma came through the door.

"Wash your hands," Ms. Novák said, and slid an empty ladle across the counter toward her.

fact: Many US colleges fill waitlist spots in May, after admitted students have sent deposits and the college knows how many places are still open.
story:
The tour group gathered under a copper beech outside the admissions building, forty students and their parents fanning themselves with folders on the first warm Saturday of April. Peyton had the folder too, though she had not opened it. She was here to look at Hartwell College, the school that had admitted her in March with a scholarship that covered most of tuition, and she was trying to look at it honestly while another school, Alden, held her name on a waitlist and gave nothing away.

She had checked the portal eleven times since Tuesday. It said the same thing each time: your application remains under consideration. No rank, no number, no hint. Her mother had started saying "Alden is not a person, you can't interrogate it," which was true, and which changed nothing.

The tour guide, a junior named Adele with a laminated badge and a practiced stride, led them across the quad. She pointed out the library, the new science building, the dining hall where, she said, the pasta station never closed. Peyton's mother wrote things down. Peyton looked at the students sprawled on the grass with their shoes off and tried to adjudicate, in her own head, whether she could be one of them, whether the question was even fair to ask of a place she'd known for ninety minutes.

At the edge of the group a boy in a green windbreaker was arguing quietly with his father. "I'm just saying we could wait," the boy said. "You said yourself they go to the waitlist in May." His father said something too low to hear, and the boy turned away and ended up walking beside Peyton as the group moved toward the residence halls.

"Sorry," he said. "You didn't need to hear that." He introduced himself as Calum. He was waitlisted at a school in Ohio, and he had figured out, from forums and an older cousin, how the timing worked. "Here's the thing," he said. "A lot of colleges fill their waitlist spots in May, after admitted students have sent in their deposits and the college finally knows how many places are still open. So you sit there until May either way. You're not finding out early. Nobody finds out early." He said it flatly, like a bus schedule, and Peyton felt something in her chest settle and tighten at the same time.

"Because deposits are due May first," she said. "So they count them, and then they know what's left." Calum nodded. "So I'd have to put a deposit down somewhere else, here for instance, and just leave it there. Four hundred dollars. Nonrefundable." She had not said the number aloud before. Her mother was three steps ahead, photographing a doorway.

They caught up to the group inside a first-year dorm, a triple with lofted beds and a window overlooking a loading dock. Adele was describing the roommate questionnaire. Peyton's mother touched her arm. "What do you think?" she asked, and Peyton understood the question underneath it, which was about money and about hope and about how long a person could responsibly hold both. Her mother was not a sagacious woman in the way of books; she was sagacious about people, about landlords and dentists and which relatives to believe, and Peyton had learned to take that kind of knowing seriously even when it came without reasons attached.

After the tour they sat on a bench near the beech tree, splitting a soft pretzel from the cart by the gate. Peyton laid it out plainly, the way Ms. Pham had taught her to lay out an argument in tenth grade, one claim at a time. She wanted Alden. Alden might call in May, or might never call. The waitlist filled after deposits came in, so waiting longer bought her nothing; the information would not arrive before the deadline that forced her hand. Hartwell was real, was here, had admitted her outright, and four hundred dollars was four hundred dollars. "I could be the dissident in my own life," she said. "Refuse the deposit on principle, wait it out, and then end up with nothing in June if Alden says no." Calum laughed once, not unkindly. "Or you could be a person who goes to college," he said.

The May deadline was two weeks away. Peyton took her phone out, opened the Hartwell portal, and let the deposit page sit on the screen while a tour group, the next one, formed under the beech and the guide lifted her folder for their attention. Her mother leaned over and looked at the screen, then at her, and waited. Peyton put her thumb on the button.
